#5561. 3 Things Sellers Need To Know About Pricing Today

If you’re getting ready to sell your house, you’ve probably heard how important it is to price it right. And that’s especially true right now.

Today’s buyers have more homes to choose from and they’re feeling pinched by today’s mortgage rates. That makes them more selective. And that means having the right pricing strategy matters more than ever.

That starts with understanding these three things. Because, with the right approach, you can still put your house in a great position to sell.

It’s natural to look at what your neighbor’s house sold for and think yours should sell for something similar. And those comparable sales (or comps) absolutely matter. But they only tell part of the story. Here’s why.

Buyers aren’t shopping against what sold three or even six months ago. They’re comparing your house to what’s available right now.

That’s why your agent will look at more than just recent sales. They’ll also consider the houses currently for sale, what’s going under contract, and how your house stacks up against those options to find the right price for your house.

The goal isn’t necessarily to price lower than everyone else. It’s to make sure buyers see the value in choosing your house over the competition.

As Jake Krimmel, Senior Economist at Realtor.com explains:

“Pricing to today’s demand is helping homes move and keeping more transactions alive in a high-rate environment.”

Understanding how your house compares to what’s available today can help you feel more confident in your asking price.

Getting your asking price right puts you in a stronger position from the start. But when an offer comes in, remember that price is only one part of the equation.

Today’s buyers may still negotiate on things like money toward closing costs or repairs, even when a house is priced well – and that’s not necessarily a commentary on your price, it’s just the norm for negotiation in today’s market.

According to Redfin, 44.7% of home sales involve seller concessions. That’s just under half. And 15.8% had both a price reduction and a concession.

Now, that doesn’t mean you have to agree to everything a buyer asks for. But sometimes offering a closing-cost credit or helping with a mortgage rate buydown could be what seals the deal. Other times, holding firm is the better move. Your agent will help you decide.

The best advice? Look at the whole offer, including what you’ll actually walk away with, to decide what’s right for you.

Even with a competitive price, some houses take longer to sell than others. And if yours isn’t getting the attention or offers you expected, that doesn’t mean your sale is off track. It just means it’s time to take a closer look at what’s happening.

Your agent can help you use buyer feedback and local market activity to figure out what adjustments, if any, could make a difference.

Are buyers seeing your listing online but not scheduling showings? Maybe the photos or presentation aren’t doing your house justice.

Are people touring but not making offers? It could be the condition, the price, or how your house compares to others they’ve seen.

And if buyers are making offers, but the terms aren’t working for you, that may call for a different negotiation strategy altogether.

While you may worry that means you have to drop your price, that’s not always true. A price cut can help, but only if it addresses what’s keeping buyers from making a move.

That’s why feedback, local competition, and an agent who knows how to interpret both are so important.

Selling successfully today isn't about finding one magic number and hoping everything falls into place. It's about starting with a competitive price, understanding what buyers expect, and being willing to adjust your strategy when needed.Want to know what it'll take to sell your house in today's market? #5560. Three insights you may have missed from theCUBE’s coverage of NetApp INSIGHT

Intelligent data infrastructure is becoming a priority as enterprises move artificial intelligence beyond isolated pilots and into production environments.

The shift places new demands on storage systems built to support traditional applications, especially as organizations introduce AI workloads across hybrid and multicloud environments. NetApp Inc. is responding with a strategy that emphasizes infrastructure modernization without requiring enterprises to abandon existing investments, according to George Kurian (pictured), chief executive officer of NetApp.

“I think that the AI era requires organizations to be really good stewards of their data, because data is the foundation for knowledge and knowledge is the intellectual property,” he told theCUBE. “To have knowledge, you need really good intelligent data infrastructure that not only allows you to extract memory and context from your data, but also to keep it secure, well governed and a resource that you can trust.”

Kurian spoke with theCUBE Research’s Christophe Bertrand and co-host Rebecca Knight during NetApp INSIGHT, in an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. The event’s coverage featured NetApp executives and technology partners discussing the evolving demands on enterprise data infrastructure and the challenges of bringing AI into production. (Disclosure below.)

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video discussion with George Kurian:

Here are three insights you may have missed from theCUBE’s coverage of NetApp INSIGHT:

Enterprise AI workloads are exposing limitations in storage architectures designed for more predictable application demands. NetApp’s Novus architecture separates data and metadata management so each can scale independently. The company’s AI Data Engine is designed to discover, classify and prepare enterprise data for AI applications, according to Syam Nair, chief product officer of NetApp.

“Performance and throughput of accessing the data, that’s a necessity for AI, but that won’t be sufficient for agents to actually act on the data,” he said during the event. “If the data is not ready and it’s not protected, you get fast results. You get compromised results, but they may not be the ones you want.”

The demands of AI factories are also changing how storage resources must be managed. NetApp’s approach aims to support high-throughput AI pipelines without sacrificing the responsiveness other applications require, according to Arindam Banerjee, chief platform and technology officer of NetApp, who spoke alongside Jason Hardy, vice president of storage technology at Nvidia Corp.

“What happens is [that] different types of workloads like transactional workloads for metadata and heavy sequential workloads for, say, checkpoints, happen at the same time,” Banerjee told theCUBE. “Previous architectures did one or the other very well. They never were able to combine it and do both at the same time.”

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video interview with Jason Hardy and Arindam Banerjee:

Modernizing enterprise infrastructure often requires organizations to accommodate existing applications while introducing new AI capabilities. NetApp and Oracle Corp. are addressing that challenge through a co-engineered, fully managed storage service that runs ONTAP natively within Oracle Cloud Infrastructure. The offering is designed to ease migration of existing ONTAP workloads without requiring application redesign, according to Konstantinos Papamiltiadis, senior vice president of partnerships at Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, a division of Oracle.

“When I’m going into the OCI console, I have the option to use the ONTAP as a native service,” he told theCUBE. “For me, the most important thing that we managed to build is, from an operational perspective, we bring everything under one single interface that provides simplicity and consistency.”

NetApp and Oracle Corp. are extending enterprise storage capabilities into the public cloud through a co-engineered, fully managed service that runs ONTAP natively within Oracle Cloud Infrastructure. The offering is designed to ease migration of existing ONTAP workloads without requiring application redesign, according to Konstantinos Papamiltiadis, senior vice president of partnerships at Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, a division of Oracle.

“When I’m going into the OCI console, I have the option to use the ONTAP as a native service,” he told theCUBE. “For me, the most important thing that we managed to build is, from an operational perspective, we bring everything under one single interface that provides simplicity and consistency.”

The integration challenge extends beyond cloud storage to the networking and compute resources that support AI workloads. NetApp and Cisco Systems Inc. are expanding their FlexPod infrastructure with validated designs intended to reduce deployment complexity. The partnership has served 10,000 customers over 16 years, according to James Cole, vice president of data center networking, business development, partnerships and go-to-market at Cisco, and Alvaro Celis, chief partner and ecosystem officer at NetApp.

“Twenty years ago, 10 years ago, you would’ve been designing your data structures and your applications around the infrastructure. Now we’ve turned that on its head,” Cole said during the event. “You’re really designing the infrastructure around the movement of data. Who better to do that together than the person you trust with your data and the person you trust with your network?”

Another partnership focuses on private AI deployment and measurable business outcomes. The NetApp AIPod Mini combines NetApp infrastructure with the Generate platform from Iterate Studio Inc., doing business as Iterate.ai, according to Brian Sathianathan, co-founder and chief technology officer of Iterate.ai. In one insurance deployment cited during the discussion, an agent reduced accident-report analysis from approximately eight hours to eight minutes.

“AIPod Mini has attached connections to the NetApp storage, and it talks to NetApp using the ONTAP protocol that’s time-tested,” he said during the event. “Then, on top of the AIPod Mini, we are running our Generate software. That software has a [large language model] embedded in it, so you can run all your AI queries locally and fully privately within your four walls.”

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video discussion with Alvaro Celis and James Cole:

As enterprises introduce autonomous agents into infrastructure management, intelligent data infrastructure must accommodate increasingly complex operational demands. NetApp’s unified control plane, delivered through NetApp Console, is designed to reduce routine administrative work through policy-driven automation. In one keynote demonstration, agents responded to a nighttime performance anomaly, according to Sandeep Singh, senior vice president and general manager of enterprise storage at NetApp.

“Agents can, in real time, implement the necessary quality of service rules to ensure there’s compliance to the boundary conditions there,” he told theCUBE. “And that way, no human is woken up. The right outcome is achieved, and there’s no noisy neighbor effect. And there’s an audit trail presented to the humans for going and following up.”

Automation, however, can’t resolve organizational questions about data ownership and responsibility. As enterprises extend intelligent data infrastructure across applications and environments, leadership must establish accountability for the information those systems rely on, according to Helen Yu, founder and chief executive officer of Tigon Advisory Corp., who appeared alongside Singh.

“It’s not a storage problem. It’s a leadership and accountability issue,” she said during the event. “When teams don’t have access to … trusted data consistently, they actually stop making decisions. They start making workarounds.”

#5559. A Mortgage Rate Buydown Could Make Your Next Home More Affordable

You want to find the right home, but you also need the right monthly payment. And that can be hard when it feels like just about everything right now is putting a squeeze on your budget.

But there’s a tool that can help, and many buyers have never heard of it – it’s called a rate buydown. Here are the basics.

When you’re borrowing money to buy a home, it usually works like this. The higher your mortgage rate, the bigger your monthly payment. And with rates where they are now, some buyers are feeling the crunch. That’s where a buydown can really come in handy.

A buydown lets you pay some money upfront to get a lower mortgage rate – and by extension a better monthly payment. Basically, it’s a way to get a lower mortgage payment without waiting for mortgage rates to fall.

There are two main types, and they work a little differently.

A temporary buydown lowers your rate for a specific amount of time – usually the first one to three years. When the buydown period is up, you begin making the full payment amount. The loan’s official rate stays the same – you’re just getting help with part of the payment in the early years.

Think of it like a gift card for your mortgage. Money goes into an escrow account at closing. Each month, part of your payment comes out of that account instead of your pocket.

Here are the most common options when it comes to temporary buydowns:

1-0 buydown: Your rate is 1% lower for the first year.

2-1 buydown: Your rate is 2% lower the first year and 1% lower the second year.

3-2-1 buydown: Your rate is 3% lower the first year, 2% lower the second, and 1% lower the third.

A permanent buydown is a bit different. The big draw here is that they last for the entire loan, which could be 15 or 30 years – not just a couple of years like a temporary buydown. But normally, the monthly savings are smaller.

It’s paid for with points. Generally, one point equals 1% of your loan amount. And each point usually lowers your rate about a quarter of a percentage, but this differs from lender to lender. The important distinction?

A temporary buydown gives you short-term payment relief.

A permanent buydown can lower your payment for as long as you keep that mortgage.

With more homes available for sale, more sellers and builders are offering incentives to attract buyers. Some are even willing to pay for your buydown.

And whether that’s advertised up front or something you ask for in negotiations, it can have a bigger impact on your bottom line than you’d think.

Take a look at this example comparing a seller-funded 2-1 buydown with a permanent buydown on a median-priced home. In this scenario, the seller would pay for the upfront buydown costs. Remember, these are estimates – your numbers will vary:

In this example, the temporary buydown provides roughly $520 in monthly payment savings during the first year, compared with about $170 a month from a permanent buydown.

That’s a big difference in the short term. But there’s an important tradeoff.

As mentioned before, the temporary buydown savings don’t last forever. Once the buydown period ends, the full mortgage payment kicks in. That’s why it’s important to compare the numbers over time, not just during the first year.

This is where a lender can really help you explore your options. A buydown isn’t automatically the best choice for every buyer. It depends on your budget, how long you plan to stay in the home, and what you’re trying to accomplish.

A temporary buydown could give you extra room in your budget during the first couple of years, when you’re also managing moving expenses and settling into your new home. And if you expect your income to go up over time, this can be a good option.

On the flipside, a permanent buydown could make more sense if you plan to stay put for years and want the reassurance that the savings are sticking around until you move.

Either way, if you’re considering a buydown, the advice is simple.

Make sure you can comfortably afford the full mortgage payment, even if you’re starting with a temporary reduction.

Factor in what it could look like if the payment goes up after the buydown period ends. You want to be sure your budget can handle it.

Remember, lenders check whether you can afford the full payment, not just the discounted amount.

If you've found a home you love but the monthly payment is giving you pause, talk to your agent about buydowns. Then, meet with your lender to see the real numbers for your situation.A buydown could give you another way to make the numbers work, especially if a seller or builder is willing to help. Who knows it may just be the difference between  "maybe someday" and "welcome home."

#5558. Mortgage Rates Dip, Offering Moderate Relief to Buyers Ahead of Thanksgiving as Fed Rate Hike Looms

Mortgage rates have pulled back this week as AI investment trade creates volatility in financial markets and Treasury yields fall back below 5%.

The average rate on 30-year fixed home loans dropped to 7.21% for the week ending Nov. 25, down 7 basis points from 7.28% recorded the week before, according to Freddie Mac. For perspective, rates averaged 6.26% one year ago.

“Mortgage rates moved back down this week, offering modest relief for prospective homebuyers heading into the Thanksgiving holiday,” says Sam Khater, Freddie Mac's chief economist.

It is all but guaranteed that the Federal Reserve will raise its benchmark rate to curb inflation at the next Federal Open Market Committee meeting on Dec. 8.

The looming hike, combined with the persistence of the war in Iran, pushed the 10-year Treasury yield back toward 4.816% this week, putting mortgage rates on an upward trajectory once again.

The AI investment trade has created volatility in financial markets as investors try to value companies, including the Anthropic IPO, which gave the company a valuation greater than the value of every home currently listed for sale.

AI-generated wealth is already shaping consumer housing behavior, with San Francisco Bay Area buyers and those in other tech hubs leaning toward higher down payments.

Markets are currently pricing a 97.6% chance of a 25-basis-point increase next month, according to the CME FedWatch tool.

Meanwhile, pending home sales fell to a record low in October, and existing-home sales hit their lowest level since 2010, as the surge in mortgage rates through mid-October took its toll on buyers and sellers.

For buyers who remain active in the market, current conditions offer some meaningful advantages, including less competition from other shoppers, inventory climbing 8.6% year over year, and sellers increasingly willing to negotiate on price.

This week, the median listing price fell 2.4% from a year ago to $400,000, according to the latest Realtor.com weekly housing market update.

"The challenge is that until inflation cools enough to put mortgage rates on a durable downward path, affordability will remain the dominant constraint on the market," says Realtor.com® senior economist Anthony Smith.

Your credit score plays a role when you apply for a mortgage. A credit score will determine whether you qualify for a mortgage and the interest rate you'll receive. The higher the credit score, the lower the interest rate you'll qualify for.

The credit score you need will vary depending on the type of loan. A score of 620 is a "fair" rating. However, people applying for a Federal Housing Administration loan might be able to get approved with a credit score of 500, which is considered a low score.

Homebuyers with credit scores of 740 or higher are typically considered to be in very good standing and can usually qualify for better rates, which can reduce monthly payments.

Tristan Navera is a senior reporter on housing policy, covering trends and solutions in the housing market from Washington, DC. He was previously a senior reporter at Bloomberg Law, and before that covered real estate for the Washington Business Journal. Earlier in his career, he spent a decade reporting on business and real estate in Dayton and Columbus, OH. A Cincinnati native, he holds a journalism degree from Ohio University.

#5557. Thinking About Taking Your House Off the Market? Read This First.

Between travel plans, family gatherings, and everything else this time of year can bring, selling your house may feel like just another squeeze on your calendar.

And if your house is already on the market, you may be wondering whether it’s worth keeping it listed. Maybe you’re even asking yourself: Wouldn’t it be easier to take a break and try again after the new year?

Before you decide, you should know there are some very real advantages that make staying on the market worthwhile.

Typically speaking, fewer people shop for homes toward the end of the year. And yes, that’s feeling even more true with rates where they are now. But here’s what you have to remember…

You don’t need dozens of people to fall in love with your house. You just need the right one. And the people who are still looking often have a pretty good reason they need to move.

Maybe they’ve accepted a new job that starts in early 2027.

Maybe their family needs more space and they’re trying to move during school breaks.

Or maybe something in their life has changed, and waiting until spring simply isn’t an option.

“Yes, things typically slow down in the weeks leading up to the holidays. But there are still people actively looking for homes and ready to pounce—or those who just entered the market on a short timeline and need to buy fast.”

The buyers looking now are exactly the types of buyers you want to see. They’re serious. They’re motivated. And they want to make this work.

Here’s another reason to think twice before taking your house off the market: other sellers may be having the exact same thought.

As the year winds down, fewer homeowners typically put their houses up for sale. And the latest data shows that’s happening again.

According to HousingWire Data, the number of new listings fell 13.4% from mid-October to mid-November 2026, and is down 7.1% year-over-year – the steepest annual decline since 2022. And that’s actually good for sellers who already have their homes listed for sale (see graph below):

For sellers who stay on the market, that means fewer of those fresh newly-listed houses to compete with. Sure, you may have other homeowners whose house has been listed for a while, but there won’t be nearly as many of those shiny, enticing “just listed” properties drawing your buyer’s attention away.

Keeping your house available gives it a chance to be seen while other homeowners are waiting for the calendar to turn. And that could mean more eyes on your house.

There’s also something to be said for keeping the momentum you’ve already built.

Your house is listed. The photos are done. Buyers can find it online. And your agent can continue marketing it to people who are actively looking.

If you take your house off the market, you could miss someone who’d be interested. But here’s the important part: staying on the market doesn’t mean you shouldn’t make adjustments.

If your house hasn’t attracted the offers you expected, this may be the perfect time to revisit your strategy.

Does the price still make sense compared to the competition?

Could better photos, staging, or a few small updates help your house stand out?

Would a price cut or upfront incentive be enough to get buyers interested?

Those are conversations worth having with your agent now, rather than assuming a new year will automatically bring a different result.

And you don’t have to put your life on hold for showings, either. Work with your agent to find a schedule that makes sense for you and your travel plans this season.

The end of the year may be busy for you, but that doesn't mean the housing market is closed for business. There are still motivated buyers looking and fewer new listings are coming onto the market.Before you decide to take your house off the market, talk to your agent about what’s happening locally and whether staying the course could help you get your house sold.

#5556. Hosting Changes How People See Their Home Designs: Survey

Group of friends celebrating at home having dinner

Hosting for the holidays can be chaos—you have to think about decorating, cooking, baking and more. But, there’s another wrench in the planning that people may forget to consider: the setup of your home. Do you have enough space? Enough parking? Enough bathrooms?

A new survey found that more and more homebuyers are taking hosting into consideration when making decisions about the design of their homes.

Homebuilder KB Home’s survey—featuring input from 2,000 U.S. adults and conducted via Talker Research—found that 58% of respondents feel that hosting has made them rethink what they want in their current or future home. While 29% of respondents said that having people over makes them feel proud of their home, 20% report that it makes them feel self-conscious.

“Hosting friends and family can highlight what people love about their homes and what they wish worked better,” said Gena Kirk, vice president of corporate design for KB Home.

As for what people are looking for, the survey reported that 35% said an open living area is the most important feature for making a home comfortable for hosting friends and family during holidays and special occasions, followed by outdoor entertaining space (30%). Other wants include a spacious kitchen (24%), an open kitchen (21%) and a large or dedicated dining area (21%).

Kirk recommended that buyers pursue new homes in order to achieve total customization.

“From spacious living areas and open floor plans to finishes that reflect personal style, a KB home works for everyday life as well as special occasions,” she said. “Our Built-to-Order approach recognizes that no two households are alike, giving buyers the flexibility to make choices that fit their lifestyle and budget and create a home that is uniquely their own.”

Hosting also inspires new priorities, as 21% of respondents said that hosting makes them think about how to make their home more welcoming or comfortable, while 25% said it makes them want to declutter or clean more often. In addition, 24% said that when they host, they notice things about their home they would want to change.

Homebuyers are gaining leverage across much of the country, but assuming every seller is ready to accept a discount could leave them misreading their local market. Read more.

#5555. Should You Wait for Lower Rates? Answers for Anyone Planning a 2027 Move.

When the family gathers around the table, the big housing headlines usually come up first. Are prices going to crash? What about a recession? (The data doesn’t point to either one.)

But by the time dessert comes out, the conversation tends to get more personal. That’s when people start talking about their own plans – whether to wait for lower rates and whether buying or selling actually makes sense right now.

Those are the questions that might shape your, your friends’, and family’s plans for 2027. So, let’s dig into each one.

Experts don’t see rates dropping much through 2027. Forecasts from Fannie Mae, the Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA), and Wells Fargo all have rates landing between about 6.9% and 7.2% by the end of next year.

So, if you’re waiting for a big drop, you could be waiting a while.

And a smaller dip may not save as much as you’d think. On a $400,000 loan, going from 7.25% to 7% lowers the monthly principal and interest payment by only about $68 (see chart below):

Odds are, that’s not as much as you expected.

The bigger opportunity is the leverage buyers have right now. Realtor.com estimates the recent rise in rates cost a buyer with a $2,000 monthly budget more than $22,000 in purchasing power. But the typical price cut on a median-priced home is about $18,000, according to HousingWire Data.

In other words, a typical price cut today can win back most of the buying power higher rates took away. That’s why the deal you can negotiate now may matter more than waiting for rates to come down.

Another lingering question, what’s going to happen to home prices going forward? Every situation is different. But if you’re ready and the numbers work for you, forecasts show buying can pay off over time.

Based on the projections of over 100 experts and economists compiled by Fannie Mae, home prices will continue to rise nationally through at least 2031. That means a $400,000 home should gain over $58,000 in value over the next 5 years (see graph below):

That’s wealth you build just by owning your home, paying down your mortgage, and if prices rise in your area. That’s a far cry from experts saying there’s going to be a crash.

And since buyers today have more homes to choose from than they’ve had in recent years, you should be able to find a home that fits your budget so you can buy now and start building that long-term wealth through the years. But since price trends vary by local market, before you start looking, talk to an agent about what’s happening where you are.

While you may be hearing that more sellers are doing price cuts or making concessions, here’s some perspective you’ll want to consider. That doesn’t mean you have to make some big compromise to get your house sold or that it’s a bad time to sell.

If you price and prep your house right, you can likely still sell fast and for a good profit. Sure, your buyer may ask for a concession, but that’s all up for negotiation – and you likely have plenty of equity to sell and come out ahead.

And don’t forget it goes both ways. Most sellers are also buyers – odds are you are too. 78% of homebuyers are repeat buyers, according to the National Association of Realtors (NAR) (see graph below). So, when you go to buy your next place, you can negotiate with that seller on terms, too.

Because if you have to be a little flexible on your sale, the sellers you buy your next house from will likely have to be flexible, too.

Right now, 43% of listings have a price cut, according to HousingWire Data. And Redfin reports nearly half of buyers are getting concessions from sellers, like help with closing costs. Those are things that will work to your benefit when it’s time to buy.

Rates aren’t expected to fall much, home prices are forecast to keep rising, and sellers usually get some flexibility back when they buy their next home. But whether to wait, buy, or sell is a big decision, and the right answer depends on your goals and your local market. If you’re weighing a move in 2027, connect with a local real estate agent to talk through your options so you can decide what’s right for you.

#5554. Cloudera launches digital sovereignty platform spanning AI and infrastructure

Cloudera Inc. today announced a digital sovereignty package that it said enables organizations to maintain control over their data, artificial intelligence models and computing infrastructure regardless of where workloads run.

Cloudera for Digital Sovereignty combines the company’s Anywhere Cloud, Open Data Lakehouse and Unified Data Fabric technologies with open-weight AI models and model customization tools from Mistral SAS, with whom Cloudera recently partnered. The integrated offering supports deployment across sovereign clouds, private data centers and fully air-gapped environments that have no connection to external networks.

“As AI becomes more autonomous and embedded in critical operations, enterprises need to know that their data, models, and infrastructure can remain under their control even as technology and regulatory requirements change,” Cloudera Chief Technology Officer Sergio Gago said in a statement.

The offering provides consistent zero-trust access controls, data lineage tracking and governance policies across deployment environments. Those capabilities are intended to help organizations address requirements imposed by the European Union’s AI Act, Digital Operational Resilience Act and Network and Information Security Directive, among other regulations.

Governance policies also extend to the enterprise data that AI agents retrieve and use in performing tasks. Mistral’s open-weight models can run alongside governed data, enabling organizations to customize models locally and execute agentic workflows without exposing sensitive information.

Cloudera’s modular hybrid cloud architecture enables users to shift computing workloads between infrastructure providers and private data centers without rewriting applications or migrating or duplicating underlying data. Organizations can also selectively apply sovereignty controls to sensitive workloads without imposing the same restrictions across their entire computing estate.

Moor Insights & Strategy Inc. Chief Analyst Patrick Moorhead said AI has raised the bar on data protection. “A company can meet every line of its sovereignty policy and still not control who accesses its data or who can turn off the models it depends on,” he said in a statement.

Cloudera said it will supplement its Mistral partnership with an ecosystem of sovereign cloud providers and implementation partners. The company is initially targeting Europe but plans to expand the partner network into other regions and regulatory jurisdictions.

Meghan Markle and Prince Harry are settling into life in their new home in the Cotswalds, and according to the Duchess of Sussex's wedding hairstylist, George Northwood, the grass is looking very green in the United Kingdom.

Northwood shared a look inside the family's latest digs in a Nov. 22 Instagram post, noting that he and Markle had recently spent quite a bit of quality time together, including a lunch date and a visit to her new property.

During an early fall trip to Markle's abode, Northwood said they "picked fruit and vegetables" from her garden. The stylist has recently welcomed a son, seven-month-old Elijah, "who has just started weaning" and is exploring new foods.

"She was very excited for all the new flavors he was going to enjoy from the garden," Northwood recalled. "I remember Archie being the same age when we went on tour to South Africa, so it was a lovely circular moment."

Later, the duo would head to The Park Restaurant—a New York-inspired eatery just blocks from Kensington Palace. In a blog on the eatery's website, Northwood divulged more about their catchup.

"I invited Meghan as she has just come back to the U.K. and, though we have stayed in touch via text, we hadn’t had the chance to have a proper download yet," Northwood said of their lunch date. "Since we last saw each other, she’s had her second baby and I’ve had my first. Catching up was like old times, when we used to have dinner together when I accompanied her on royal tours around the world."

Northwood added that Markle—who he refers to as "M"—is a wonderful lunch companion because she is "someone with good chat who enjoys a laugh and, crucially, who wants to share the food so that I get to try a bit of everything."

The pals enjoyed sea bass, French fries, and key lime pie. Northwood noted that "Meghan was happy to go along" with his pescatarian diet.

He also noted that "there is a lot of baby chat" given his recent "solo surrogacy journey," and that he's picked up plenty of "parenting tips" from the mom of two.

Northwood also shared a sweet photo of Markle smiling with his son at her home, posed beside a basket of colorful garden-picked veggies.

Markle, 45, and Harry, 42, are reported to be residing in a property on an estate belonging to their close friends, according to the Daily Mail.

They first made plans to establish a private residence in the U.K. in August of this year, six years after quitting their roles as working members of the British royal family to relocate to a $14.7 million home in Montecito, CA.

Although it was recently reported that the seemingly unexpected move was motivated by visa troubles for Harry—with a US government source telling Page Six "his visa expired and wasn't immediately renewed"—the couple's spokesperson denied the claim, telling Newsweek it is "entirely false."

In an October interview with GQ, Harry expressed that the decision was driven by a desire to seek out "opportunities for the family."

"Being able to put the kids in a British school has meant a lot to me," he said of Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5. "I didn't know how important it was to me. I always thought it was going to be something that we would try and do, but now they’ve been in school for two weeks. They’re loving it and it’s just giving them a whole different experience."

He also admitted that "it's nice to be back" on "U.K. soil for longer than a few days or a week here or there."

The family plans to stay put for the holidays, marking the children's first British Christmas.

During a Nov. 20 appearance on the British morning show, "This Morning," Harry revealed the family's plans for Thanksgiving and Christmas, noting that mother-in-law Doria Ragland will be joining them.

"My wife is very good in the kitchen and so is my mother-in-law, so I'll leave that to them," he said, noting that he hopes turkey and gumbo are on the menu.

The decision to stay in England for the holidays also comes from a desire to keep things simple during a difficult time for Markle's family, as her estranged father, Thomas Markle Sr., has been indicted in Florida on two counts of possession of child pornography.

"Everything going on with her dad is still weighing heavily on her," a source told People. "She wants the holidays to be as quiet and enjoyable as possible for the family.

"Traveling back and forth would be too much for everyone," the source added.

#5552. Industrial internet of things satellite platform Myriota raises $40M to scale its constellation and expand

Australia-based Myriota Pty. Ltd., a global satellite platform for the industrial internet of things, today announced it has raised $40 million in the first portion of its Series C to launch next-generation satellites and accelerate customer adoption across international markets.

Main Sequence Ventures, Hostplus and Australia’s National Reconstruction Fund Corporation co-led the round. Funds SA joined as a new investor. The round raised the company’s total funding to more than $107.5 million, and is expected to close in early 2027.

Founded in 2015, Myriota’s platform makes satellite connectivity commercially viable for large-scale industrial IoT, using the same core technology to track mining equipment and trailers to also monitor fuel tanks, livestock water supplies and off-grid solar.

The company’s platform combines satellite connectivity, low-power devices, field installation tools and fleet management software to support existing infrastructure. The objective is to provide access to communication tools that connect what is in place with turnkey service, so a company can connect devices, machines and smart sensors no matter how remote they are.

“We’re at the beginning of a fundamental shift in industrial IoT,” Chief Executive Ben Cade said. “Industries increasingly rely on data from the field to make decisions about their operations, assets and resources, and as AI moves into the physical world, that data becomes even more essential.”

The company expanded its platform over the past 12 months with the launch of HyperPulse, a global 5G non-terrestrial network, or NTN, and terrestrial service, and AssetHawk, a rugged, long-life asset tracker designed to make it economical to track industrial objects.

Alongside the expansion, it also grew into new verticals such as industrial fuels. It monitors and tracks fuel deployments across North America and Latin America, with EMEA and Asia Pacific to follow.

Myriota competes in a sector led by established operators such as Iridium Communications Inc., Orbcomm Inc. and Viasat Inc., alongside a growing field of providers pursuing cheaper, standards-based connections for industrial sensors and trackers.

The company said it intends to use the funds to expand its space infrastructure, including developing and launching its next-generation satellites.

#5551. Infamous ‘Hoarders’ Mansion in North Carolina Sells for $3.85 Million After Jaw-Dropping Restoration

A stunning 1929 English Tudor home in Greensboro, NC, that gained notoriety after it appeared in "Hoarders" closed last week for $3.85 million after two years on the market.

The home was built during the Gilded Age for prominent local businessman Julian Price, and designed by New York architect Charles C. Hartmann.

The 8,616-square-foot home, found at 301 Fisher Park Circle in Greensboro, has over 30 rooms, including eight bedrooms, six full bathrooms, and two half bathrooms.

The Julian Price Home was put on the National Register of Historic Place in 1980, it gained attention in 2017, when it was featured on an episode of A&E’s "Hoarders".

The home was owned, at the time, by interior designer Sandra Cowart. She had lived in the home since 1975, and kept the home in pristine condition for years, even giving tours and renting out rooms, according to a 2017 article from the Chicago Tribune.

After 2005, she became closed off, became a compulsive collector, and her home was ultimately foreclosed on. The home was purchased out of foreclosure by Eric and Michael Fuko-Rizzo for $415,000, a fraction of the property’s value.

The couple transformed the home back to its former glory with their deep knowledge and love of old homes and architecture.

“They were great people to re-do it, Eric and Michael. Michael’s energy and knowledge of loving old places is honestly over the top,” listing agent Kay Chesnutt, of Berkshire Hathaway Home Services, told Realtor.com. “Not many people would even consider redoing something or saving something like that.”

In addition to its numerous bedrooms, the home has an elaborate butlers' pantry, library, great room, and breakfast room. For sunny North Carolina days, there  is also a sunroom and a screened porch. All of the details were restored with intention and care for the home’s history.

“It’s like walking into a magical part of history. The beauty of the details and how they were restored—or, if they had to remove something, they’d replicate it,” Chesnutt described the restoration process. “It is something that should be saved for Greensboro. Anybody that goes into it says ‘Wow,’ because the pictures don’t even do it justice.

After the restoration, the Fuko-Rizzos opened the home up as an inn. At times, the home would be rented out in its entirety by families or host community events. It even received visits from stars like Carrie Underwood and Leanne Morgan, according to Chesnutt.

“Unwind in our drawing room with a book and glass of wine while observing the detail of the original molded plaster ceiling and fireplace surround,” the inn’s website reads. “However you plan your visit, it is certain that the charm, elegance and restored original details of this 1929 Tudor mansion will captivate and leave you and your guests with lasting memories.”

The Fuko-Rizzos listed the home for sale again in August of 2024, for an initial price of $5.25 million.

The property’s operation as an inn is one of the reasons that such a stunning home would remain on the market for two years, Chesnutt said. As the listing agent, she and the owners would have to coordinate showings around room availability.

“We couldn’t show it when there were people that were registered and paying guests. Their rooms were locked, so we only showed it when times were open, and it was empty and clean and always immaculate,” said Chesnutt.

After over two years, the home closed on November 19 for $3.85 million. The new owners are a local couple.

“It just suited them,” said Chesnutt. “And I think they’ll be good care takers.”

Chesnutt could not disclose whether the the new owners plan to keep the property open as an inn or make it a family home, but the property is no longer active on Airbnb. Either way, the Julian Price Home has a long life ahead of it due to good bones and quality craftsmanship.

“It has a wonderful feeling, and even on the darkest days, it’s very light,” said Chesnutt. “And the quality that was done then, we couldn’t reproduce today.”

Why is crypto down again? The cryptocurrency market is firmly in the red on Wednesday, November 25, 2026. Total market capitalization has slipped to around $2.02 trillion, down roughly 1.8–2% over the past 24 hours, while the Fear & Greed Index sits deep in Extreme Fear territory near 13/100.

Traders are growing disillusioned with the crypto market after weeks of downside sell pressure that has seen Bitcoin crash nearly -30% to under $60,000. Many are left wondering what could reverse the market’s course as we head toward 2027.

Bitcoin (BTC) is trading near $58,000–$58,400, down approximately 3% on the day and struggling to regain the $60,000 level after briefly testing higher earlier in the week.

Ethereum (ETH) sits around $1,630–$1,640, off about 3.3–3.5%. Solana (SOL) is softer still at roughly $66.80–$67.30, down around 4%. XRP is near $0.89–$0.90 (down ~2.5%), and BNB trades around $533–$536 (down ~2.5%).

Most other large-cap altcoins are also lower, reflecting weak market breadth. These levels follow Bitcoin’s failure to hold gains sparked by the recent Nvidia-related rebound, leaving the market on the back foot heading into month-end.

The primary driver remains persistent institutional selling through U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs. November has already set a record for monthly outflows, with figures ranging from about $4.71Bn to nearly $5Bn depending on the data provider.

BlackRock’s IBIT has led the redemptions on multiple sessions, including large single-day withdrawals exceeding $500M earlier in the week and continued outflows of roughly $230M more recently. What was once a reliable source of demand has flipped into a consistent headwind.

Broader risk-off sentiment is amplifying the pressure. A sharp sell-off in Asian markets, including a roughly 6% drop in South Korea’s KOSPI and heavy losses for SoftBank, spilled into global risk assets. Technology and AI-related stocks, which had briefly rallied on news of Jensen Huang’s reinstatement at Nvidia, quickly faded.

Crypto continues to trade as a high-beta risk asset, moving closely with equities as investor risk appetite contracts. Macro factors are also weighing heavily. Markets are pricing in high odds of a Federal Reserve rate hike in December, with elevated Treasury yields reducing the relative appeal of non-yielding assets like Bitcoin.

Reports of potential new U.S. tariffs targeting multiple trading partners have added another layer of uncertainty. Thin liquidity around the Thanksgiving holiday period may also be magnifying moves.

In short, the market faces a classic mix of sustained ETF outflows, cooling equity momentum, tighter monetary-policy expectations, and residual geopolitical/trade noise. Sentiment has deteriorated to the point where any bounce is being sold rather than chased.

Despite the heavy atmosphere, several catalysts could stabilize or reverse the decline. Today’s U.S. economic data, particularly PCE inflation and GDP figures, will be closely watched.

Softer-than-expected readings that reduce the probability of aggressive Fed tightening could quickly improve risk appetite across stocks and crypto. A slowdown or reversal in ETF outflows would be an important positive signal.

Even a return to modest net inflows would suggest institutional selling is exhausting and that larger players are beginning to accumulate at these lower levels.

On-chain data has already shown some large-wallet accumulation in recent weeks even as ETF products bled, hinting that longer-term holders may be positioning ahead of a potential recovery.

Bitcoin and Ethereum look deeply oversold on shorter timeframes, with RSI readings in the low-to-mid 20s in some analyses. Extreme fear readings have historically preceded relief rallies, especially when price approaches prior support zones.

Any constructive regulatory development, clearer institutional adoption news, or a rebound in technology stocks could also help shift momentum. Thinner holiday liquidity means volatility is likely to remain elevated in either direction.

While the near-term setup remains cautious and further downside is possible if risk assets continue to weaken, extreme sentiment, oversold technical conditions, and potential macro relief provide a plausible path to stabilization once the current wave of selling pressure eases.

Crypto markets have repeatedly demonstrated resilience after periods of heavy institutional outflows and macro headwinds; whether that pattern reasserts itself in the coming sessions will depend heavily on the data and a shift in broader risk appetite.

#5549. Regional Spotlight: California Home Sales Hit Lowest Level as Prices, Mortgage Rates Rise

(TNS)–As the year comes to an end, California’s housing market has slowed down.

Existing home sales have dropped to their lowest level in nearly three years as high mortgage rates and affordability challenges continue.

“Homebuying activity weakened across California in October, pushing sales to their lowest level in nearly three years as elevated mortgage rates and low affordability remained significant hurdles for prospective buyers,” the California Association of Realtors said in its latest housing report, released on Tuesday, Nov. 17.

Existing single-family home sales totaled 246,830 in October.

That is a decrease of 5.2% from the 260,410 sales in September and 12.7% from the 282,760 sales in October 2025.

“When mortgage rates jumped to a nearly three-year high in late September, we saw many buyers step back and reassess what they could afford, which led to fewer closed sales in October,” California Association of Realtors President Mark Peterson said in the report.

Despite the slowdown in sales, real estate experts said, home prices remained relatively steady, while mortgage rates continued to pose a challenge for potential buyers.

What can California homebuyers expect to pay?

Here’s what to know about home prices, mortgage rates and where buyers can find more affordable options across the state:

How much does buying a home cost in California?

The statewide median home price was $886,760 in October, according to the California Association of Realtors.

That was down 1.4% from $899,720 in September but barely changed from $887,330 in October 2025.

California’s median home price previously reached a record $930,260 in May.

“Home prices held steady, suggesting that buyers are still engaged and sellers remain confident in the value of their homes despite the near-term slowdown,” Peterson said.

Still, affordability remains a major obstacle for many prospective homebuyers across the state.

How much are current mortgage rates in California?

Mortgage rates continued to climb in October, adding to the challenges facing homebuyers, according to the California Association of Realtors.

The group’s report put the average mortgage rate at 7.33%—up from the 6.86% in September and 6.25% in October 2025.

Zillow listed the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate in California at about 7.38%, as of Thursday, Nov. 19.

The combination of higher borrowing costs and economic uncertainty could continue to weigh on home sales in the coming year, according to Jordan Levine, the California Association of Realtors’ senior vice president and chief economist.

“The housing market is facing renewed headwinds as inflation remains elevated and the stock market loses momentum,” Levine said in the housing report. “Home sales will likely remain soft in the near term, but pent-up demand continues to build as many prospective buyers stay on the sidelines.”

If geopolitical tensions and economic uncertainty ease, Levine said, California “should see more of those buyers gradually return to the market.”

Where can I find homes under $400,000 in California?

Despite California housing some of the most expensive home prices in the country, some counties still have median home prices below the statewide median of $886,760.

According to the California Association of Realtors, the state’s most affordable homes can be found in Northern California, with a median price of $385,000.

However, one Central Valley county offers home costs as low as $288,000.

#5548. Key insights from HPE’s Q4 earnings report

ANALYSIS by Zeus Kerravala

Hewlett Packard Enterprise Co.delivered a record fiscal fourth quarter this week, roughly doubling its fiscal 2027 growth outlook, but its stock gave back nearly all of the prior day’s rally. The selloff suggests Wall Street still prices HPE as a low-margin server vendor, even though the results describe a networking and artificial intelligence infrastructure company with demand exceeding its ability to ship.

Fourth-quarter revenue rose 50%, to $14.5 billion, orders grew 88%, and adjusted earnings of $1.43 per share topped the high end of guidance. HPE now expects fiscal 2027 revenue to grow 27% to 35%, with adjusted earnings of $5.05 to $5.35 per share, according to its earnings release.

I joined a briefing with Chief Executive Antonio Neri and a small group of independent analysts shortly before the results came out. Here are my four takeaways for investors and information technology leaders:

Neri explained that networking orders grew more than 4.5 times faster than networking revenue in the quarter, up from 3.5 times the quarter before, and HPE exited the year with $10.5 billion in AI backlog.

HPE doubled its networking purchase commitments over the summer and raised them again in the fourth quarter, but those components carry lead times of 28 to 40-plus weeks, so Neri expects networking conversion to pick up starting in the second quarter. Supply constraints are a better problem to have than weak demand, but they mean fiscal 2027 hinges on converting orders rather than winning them.

The Juniper Networks integration is complete, and the annual cost-synergy target has risen to $800 million, but the bigger story remains the profit mix. Chief Financial Officer Marie Myers said networking will account for more than 40% of HPE’s operating profit by the fourth quarter of fiscal 2027, up from less than a quarter of revenue. AI is a major driver, with routing orders growing by triple digits as customers connect AI data centers to one another.

Security was the soft spot, which Neri called “just timing.” When I asked whether the security portfolio is where he wants it as the industry consolidates around big platforms, he argued for a different path.

“Fortinet and we have a different strategy — the convergence of security and networking — and we are taking it all the way down to the silicon level,” he said. The convergence of networking and security is underway but will take time to execute, as a considerable amount of technical debt must go through its depreciation cycle. In a greenfield situation, organizations can easily deploy a converged solution, but in a brownfield environment, it requires much more work. This is the right strategy, but it remains a “prove-it” business for HPE.

Many neoclouds rely on vendor financing and chip-backed debt, raising real concerns about who is left exposed if the buildout slows. HPE says it has stayed out, and Neri was quite emphatic about it on the briefing.

“I want to be clear: We have not financed any neocloud through HPFS, our financing arm,” he said. “We have zero exposure to any AI financing for neocloud.” HPE has likely left some revenue on the table, but it drew the line in the right place. It will sell to neoclouds, as its $1.2 billion Vultr order shows, without acting as their bank. Enterprise and sovereign customers account for the majority of its cumulative AI orders, and if the neocloud financing chain breaks, HPE’s financing arm won’t be the one holding the paper.

Training built the first phase of AI infrastructure, and Neri believes inference will build the next and will dominate demand for AI infrastructure. “I believe by the end of the decade, 80% will be in AI inferencing,” he said. “Much of that will land on-prem. Much of that will be distributed, for sure. That’s why the server business is structurally well-positioned.”

Once agents are in production, token costs become a recurring bill, and companies will want inference running alongside their own data. Those servers require far more memory and pull in storage and services, which is better business than racking graphics processing units for a hyperscaler.

Evidence of this is the interest in Helios, the Advanced Microdevices Inc. rack that uses HPE’s Ethernet switching rather than Nvidia’s proprietary interconnect. I asked Neri whether Jensen Huang’s brief departure from Nvidia Corp. had opened that door. He said interest was building before then, as customers look to diversify.

HPE shares jumped 17% on Monday ahead of the report as part of a broader AI rally, then fell about 13% in early trading on Tuesday, ending near where they started the week. I see three reasons for this.

The first is margins. Cloud & AI operating margin was 18.4% in the quarter, and HPE guided to about 14% for fiscal 2027. Reuters reported that JPMorgan analysts called margin mix the key debate for investors.

The second is pricing. Myers said higher selling prices have been the biggest driver of server growth, and she expects gross margin to moderate in the second half as AI server volumes ramp and costs rise faster than pricing.

The third is timing. HPE expects about 54% of revenue in the second half, with the ramp tied to Helios shipments, the Oracle Corp. deal, customer data center readiness and component supply. Those are fair execution questions, but they miss the shift in where HPE’s profit comes from.

On the topic of margins, the 18.4% came off an unusual stretch of favorable pricing that should not have been modeled as permanent. Neri argued the guide is still “significantly higher than any historical margin we have had in this business,” and he’s right outside the past year. A year ago, the segment’s margin was 9.3%. Margin rate also isn’t margin dollars. At 30% to 40% revenue growth, my math shows Cloud & AI adding well over $1 billion in operating profit at the midpoint.

The bears are right that price-driven server growth doesn’t warrant a premium multiple, which is why the mix matters more. The market is fixated on the segment whose margins are normalizing and ignoring the one whose margins are expanding. Adjusted earnings per share are still guided to grow by 27% to 35%, in line with revenue growth. That’s far from the margin doom-and-gloom narrative on the stock.

The back-half concern is real but manageable. Myers described the pipeline as multiples of the backlog, and Neri said the guide assumes only historical win rates against it.

Then there’s quality. HPE is guiding to about 30% growth and at least $5.5 billion in free cash flow, has no neocloud financing exposure and has already brought leverage below its target. It trades at about eight times the midpoint of its adjusted earnings guidance. “I don’t see us at a multiple that is 8 to 9x; it makes no sense whatsoever,” Neri said on the earnings call.

For old HPE, that’s true, as it’s a server vendor, but HPE is increasingly a network vendor each quarter. In fact, during our pre-call with Neri, he led with networking and spoke at length about the business before pivoting to the server business. Expect networking to continue to drive a larger share of profits.

Fiscal 2027 is an execution year. HPE must convert purchase commitments into shipments, ramp Helios and prove that networking margins can climb even as cloud and AI margins settle. I’ll be watching networking order conversion more closely than server margins. If HPE executes, today’s multiple will prove to be too low.

Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

#5547. Judge Upholds Mamdani’s NYC Rent Freeze, Tosses Landlords’ Lawsuit

A Manhattan judge has upheld New York City's rent freeze for roughly 1 million rent-stabilized apartments, dismissing a lawsuit brought by landlords who argued that the decision was politically predetermined.

In a 20-page ruling issued on Wednesday, New York Supreme Court Justice Brendan T. Lantry found that the city's Rent Guidelines Board had acted within its authority when it voted this summer to freeze rents on both one- and two-year leases.

The landlords, led by Kenilworth Holdings LLC, argued that Mayor Zohran Mamdani had effectively dictated the outcome after campaigning on a promise to freeze rents and appointing board members who supported the policy.

Despite the favorable ruling, Lantry wasn't entirely sympathetic to the mayor. In his final decision, he called Mamdani's campaign promise "reckless and irresponsible." Even so, he concluded that the board had independently considered the evidence before reaching its decision.

The freeze passed in June after a landmark 7-1 vote, with only Arpit Gupta, an economist who was appointed to the board in 2022 by Mayor Eric Adams, voting no.

But it was owner-representative Maksim Wynn's statement that stoked controversy at the meeting, after he raised concerns about the financial health of the city's buildings. Wynn's full statement was drowned out by boos from the crowd before he ultimately voted in favor of the freeze.

Those pressures were central to the landlords' suit, which argued that a "rent freeze is impossible to reconcile" with such rising costs, pointing to mounting expenses for insurance, maintenance, utilities, and property taxes.

Operating and maintenance expenses consumed roughly 71 cents of every dollar of revenue in 2024, according to the board's 2026 Income and Expense Study. And as Realtor.com® previously reported, those figures exclude mortgage payments and major capital expenses, which landlords argue can leave otherwise profitable-looking buildings struggling financially.

“Freezing rent sounds like a sure-fire way to solve housing affordability, but what I'm worried about is the unintended consequences on the rent-stabilized stock and market-rate prices,” Jake Krimmel, senior economist at Realtor.com, said in June.

Lantry acknowledged that potential fallout, writing that the freeze could have "detrimental impacts on the New York City residential real estate industry." But he emphasized that weighing the wisdom of the policy was not the court's role, writing that the freeze "has a rational basis and must therefore be upheld as valid."

The ruling leaves the freeze intact; however, the landlords could seek to appeal.

#5546. Congress scrutinizes Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia as Megaspeed restrictions raise questions

Lawmakers on both sides of the aisle are criticizing Nvidia Corp.’s decision to rehire Jensen Huang as its chief executive.

The criticism came against the backdrop of a controversial move by the U.S. Commerce Department. The agency applied new export restrictions to Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud operator. The company played a prominent role in the spy controversy that led to Huang’s resignation. According to trade experts, the Commerce Department left out a key clause that is usually included in such restrictions.

Huang resigned on Nov. 12 following revelations that he had an affair with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive. Early reporting about the relationship indicated that she was found to have passed intelligence to China. The U.S. Justice Department later stated that it has not yet reached a conclusion on whether Alice Huang is a spy. Earlier this week, the New York Times reported that she maintained contact with a Chinese intelligence official.

Nvidia’s board reinstated Jensen Huang on Monday after U.S. President Donald Trump and tech industry figures urged directors to bring him back. The move drew widespread criticism from members of Congress.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-New York), who is set to become House Speaker, called the reinstatement “indefensible, irresponsible and incomprehensible.” Rep. Don Bacon (R-Nebraska), the chair of House Subcommittee on Cyber, Information Technologies and Innovation, said that “it’s inexplicable to me why they want this guy back as CEO.” Former Utah Republican Senator and Massachusetts Governor Mitt Romney tweeted: “Let me get this straight: we rushed AI along without regulating safeguards in order to stay ahead of China and at the same time, we sold China the very chips they’d need to get ahead of us. Smells of profit, corruption and perhaps worse.”

Multiple lawmakers told CNBC that they plan to scrutinize Huang’s conduct closely. The executive is scheduled to testify before multiple Congressional committees next Tuesday. Furthermore, Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Oregon) told the outlet that Democrats plan to scrutinize the Trump administration’s role in the matter.

The Commerce Department today added Megaspeed and several of its regional affiliates to its Entity List. Companies on the list can only purchase sensitive products such as graphics cards if they obtain a license from the U.S. government. According to Gizmodo, the move has drawn scrutiny because the restrictions applied to Megaspeed include a loophole.

All the companies on the Entity List are prohibited from buying Nvidia’s latest chips unless they secure a license. Most of them are also unable to buy lower-end graphics cards, high-bandwidth memory and related hardware. The latter restrictions are specified in a clause called the FDPR provision. The Commerce Department has reportedly not applied the FDPR provision to Megaspeed when it added the company to the Entity List.

Huang returned to Nvidia’s Santa Clara headquarters on Monday. The news sent the chipmaker’s stock soaring more than 30%, although it parred some of the gains today. Nvidia shares are down 5.8% from Monday.

Wired today published excerpts from Huang’s all-hands meeting with employees. The executive apologized for his affairs and for his management style, which has also come under scrutiny in recent days. He added that he will undergo a “360-degree review” and that Nvidia’s code of conduct is still in effect.

#5545. From Mold Poisoning to Lyme Disease: Inside the Extreme Moves 6 Stars Made to Save Their Health

In many cases, a health diagnosis can be life-changing. From dealing with symptoms to navigating treatment, managing medical issues is no easy feat.

And while accessibility upgrades and wellness integrations can certainly make a home more habitable in these instances, some people choose to pack up and move altogether—particularly celebrities.

Of course, celebrities may also have the means to relocate when particular symptoms could be managed more easily in a different climate.

Although some high profile individuals prefer to keep these kinds of decisions close to the chest, a handful of celebs have spoken candidly about the health-related circumstances that inspired them to migrate.

Jenny McCarthy and Donnie Wahlberg recently offloaded their longtime Illinois residence for $2.6 million. The transaction comes just as “The Masked Singer” host has publicly shared her experience dealing with the effects of “mold and mycotoxin poisoning.”

During the Oct. 28 episode of “The Jenny McCarthy Wahlberg Show,” she revealed that she’s been living in a tent after undergoing the costly experience of remediating her home.

In a later episode, McCarthy also noted that she has discarded all of her clothing and furniture in a continued attempt to escape the mold.

In the wake of the ordeal, she’s considering a relocation.

“I’m so paranoid that I’ve even talked to Donny about moving out of the midwest, where it’s humid, and going to a dry location like Vegas or Arizona or something, because my body just can’t detox mold very well,” McCarthy said.

McCarthy and Wahlberg have yet to make a permanent move, but the sale of their St. Charles property could certainly be the first step towards change.

Retired Major League Baseball star Matt Holliday and his wife, Leslie Holliday, were left with no choice but to leave the dream home they’d built in Stillwater, OK, when he was diagnosed with a respiratory disease.

“The doctor said he needed to get to dry climate quick,” listing agent Vincent Clark told the Phoenix Business Journal.

Clark is the agent representing the sale of the Paradise Valley, AZ property the Hollidays initially relocated to.

They purchased the $10.6 million home in February of this year after the World Series champion received the diagnosis a week after a water leak had affected their 136-acre custom home in Oklahoma, which is still on the market for $8.95 million.

While the sprawling Arizona property was well-equipped with “substantial healthy-home enhancements” including air and water filtration and conditioning systems, Clark revealed that the Hollidays are seeking a home with an existing guest house, although the 7,781-square-foot home they’re hoping to sell includes transferred approved plans for an 845-square-foot guest casita.

In an Aug.10 social media post, “The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives” alum Mikayla Matthews admitted that her “home situation is always up in the air.”

The reality TV personality was diagnosed with Chronic Inflammatory Response Syndrome (CIRS), which she believes was triggered by extended exposure to mold-related toxins.

She and her family spent much of 2026 traveling in hopes of easing her symptoms, and temporarily relocated to Hawaii in May before heading to Florida in June in pursuit of a humid climate.

“The heavy metals in the air from Great Salt Lake drying up add to my toxic load everyday, so I can’t detox everything out,” she wrote in an Instagram post.

In October, Matthews revealed that her family was leaving the home she says was “making” her “sick,” and had purchased a new home in Utah, which is still under construction.

Bella Hadid recently purchased an idyllic $5.5 million home in Colorado, but it’s not the first time she’s snapped up a property with a stunning connection to nature.

In 2024, the model spoke to Allure about her decision to take a break from the industry in pursuit of a more laid back lifestyle in Fort Worth, TX, citing mental health struggles including severe anxiety and brain fog, as well as her longtime battle with Lyme disease.

The move marked a focus on her mental and physical health, as well as a dedication to a passion she’d lost with fame: horseback riding.

At the time, Hadid was dating Adan Banuelos, an equestrian trainer. The pair were seemingly on and off for two years before separating earlier in 2026, but during their time together, she began competing in amateur cutting horse competitions after a history as a longtime show jumper.

Musician Taylor Dayne decided to trade a life in Los Angeles for a slower pace in Santa Barbara after recovering from stage two colon cancer.

The “Tell It To My Heart” singer considered the move to be part of her healing process.

“I loved the idea of living in this sanctuary. It’s pretty magical up here,” she said to the Montecito Journal. “I am really relishing being in a sacred space where everybody is pretty damn happy.”

Dayne told People magazine that she’s feeling healthy four years after her diagnosis in July of this year.

“So far, so good,” she said of her health. “All clean.”

Actress Jamie Lynn Sigler was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis in her early 20s, and kept it private for nearly 15 years before revealing the diagnosis in 2016.

During the Covid-19 pandemic, “The Sopranos” star and her husband, Cutter Dyktra, left California with their two sons, Beau and Jack, and relocated to Texas.

“We needed a change. When I moved here, I started using a cane once in a while because I didn’t feel like I was being watched,” she told Us magazine. “Here, it was like, ‘I’m just Beau and Jack’s mom at the baseball field.’”

The mom of two has shared that her family is fully embracing their new life.

“I feel disconnected, in the best way I’ve ever known,” she told People magazine. “It’s all about outdoors and nature which I really appreciate since I never had it growing up in New York and L.A.”

#5544. Workday shares fall as soft subscription forecast overshadows third-quarter beat

Shares of human resources and finance software company Workday Inc. fell more than 7% in late trading today after a softer-than-expected subscription revenue forecast for the current quarter overshadowed fiscal third-quarter earnings and revenue that came in ahead of Wall Street’s targets.

For the quarter that ended on Oct. 31, Workday reported adjusted earnings per share of $2.82, up 22% from $2.32 in the same quarter of the previous year, on revenue of $2.705 billion, up 11.2% year-over-year. Analysts were expecting earnings of $2.75 per share on revenue of $2.69 billion.

Subscription revenue rose 12.8% from a year earlier, to $2.532 billion. Net income on an unadjusted basis came to $237 million, down from $252 million in the same quarter a year ago. Included in the quarter were $51 million in restructuring expenses, which followed the company’s disclosure in late September that it would cut about 2.5% of its workforce, mostly in its product and technology team.

Total subscription revenue backlog grew 6.1%, to $27.548 billion, with the 12-month figure up 12.3%, to $9.216 billion. Free cash flow came to $691 million, up from $550 million. During the quarter, Workday spent $750 million buying back about 3.8 million shares.

The quarter also saw Workday hold its annual Rising customer conference in Las Vegas in October, when the company made Sana the new home experience for its platform. Built on technology from Sana Labs AB, which Workday acquired for about $1.1 billion last year, Sana is an AI interface that brings tasks, decisions, meetings and agent activity together in one place. Autopilot Agents, also launched at the event, are designed to handle routine HR, finance and IT processes in the background.

On the opening day of Rising, Workday announced that it had agreed to acquire agentic identity platform ConductorOne Inc., better known as C1.ai. That deal closed on Monday. A partnership with Anthropic PBC, also unveiled at Rising, is set to bring Claude together with Sana AI agents and Workday’s HR and finance data.

“The past few quarters have been our strongest on the innovation and invention front, and in Q3, our AI products drove nearly $150 million in new ACV, more than three times what we delivered a year ago,” said co-founder and Chief Executive Aneel Bhusri, who returned to the top job in February after Carl Eschenbach stepped down. The priority now, Bhusri added, is to get more customers running agents in production.

According to Workday, the number of core customers that have bought at least one of its AI products rose nearly 25% from the previous quarter, to more than 2,200.

Pointing to what he called “ongoing adoption across our AI portfolio,” Chief Financial Officer Zane Rowe said the company is raising its full-year targets.

For its fiscal fourth quarter, Workday expects subscription revenue of $2.6 billion, up 10%, and an adjusted operating margin of 31.7%. Full-year subscription revenue is now forecast at $9.958 billion, up 13%, compared with the $9.94 billion to $9.95 billion guided in August. The full-year adjusted operating margin forecast was also raised, to 31.5%, ahead of the 31.1% expected by analysts.

Though the full-year numbers moved higher, the fourth-quarter subscription forecast came in narrowly below the $2.61 billion analysts had been expecting. Growth of 10% in the period would also be a step down from the 12.8% Workday posted in the third quarter.

Workday Chief Technology Officer Gabe Monroy made the case for taking agents to where employees already work during an interview in August. Speaking with theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio, for the Google Cloud: AI Agents in Action series, Monroy said enterprise agents need the deterministic rules of a system like Workday to go with the probabilistic reasoning of AI. “We don’t want to ask customers to have to switch their front doors or log into Workday when they’re happy to use Gemini systems,” he said.
