#5407. 10 last-minute Black Friday tricks to check before you pay today

A selection of 10 Black Friday tricks for shoppers heading out today, and how to check each one against the price before you pay

If you're shopping today, the sale price doesn't have to be the final price. You can sometimes shave off more with a card that earns rewards, cash back after the fact, a promo code or a free gift. Black Friday falls on Friday, Nov. 27, this year, so there's no weekend left to plan. Whatever checking you do will happen in the aisle or on your phone.

That checking matters, because the extras don't always stack. Rakuten's own help center warns that using a coupon code the site doesn't list can void your cash back. It also notes that some stores won't pay cash back on any part of a purchase covered by a gift card. Pile on every trick at once and you can end up worse off than someone who picked one carefully. The real skill today is knowing which extra to use on which purchase, not grabbing all of them.

The headline offer rarely tells the whole story, either. Some retailers don't bother waiting for Friday. Target's Black Friday sale started Sunday, Nov. 22, so a "Black Friday deal" you see there today may have been sitting there for days. The flashiest perks often come with strings. Target's in-store gift card giveaway went only to the first 100 people in line at each store, who received cards worth $25, $50 or $100. One person per store got a $1,000 card, and tickets had to be redeemed within an hour of the 6 a.m. opening. Discounted gift cards are everywhere this week too. KCRA reports offers like up to 25% off at Sam's Club and up to 20% off select cards at Best Buy. But a discounted gift card only saves you money if it's for a store you'll actually shop at.

NBC News Select's Black Friday guide lays out the main ways to cut costs. They include discounted gift cards, cash-back portals and apps, rewards credit cards, gifts with purchase, price-history trackers and price-adjustment policies. Some of these quietly hand back money on things you were going to buy anyway. Others work better as warnings about how retailers dress up a price. Either way, each one only pays off on top of a price you've already checked. That's the test every tactic here has to pass.

A discounted gift card doesn't lower the price of any one product. It lowers the cost of the money you pay with, so the saving lands on top of whatever markdown is already on the shelf. Pay $90 for a $100 card and you've knocked another $10 off, while still getting the store's own sale price. The catch is that the card only works at a store that takes it. That means you pick the store first and the card second. A cheap card for a store you weren't planning to visit just ties up your money. If you're still shopping this weekend, buy a card only for a store that's already on your list, not a stack of cheap cards on the off chance you'll use them.

How much you save depends on which card you buy and where you buy it. On Black Friday, Bass Pro Shops and Cabela's were taking 10% off holiday gift cards, and inKind cards were 30% off on Amazon, KCRA reported. The Amazon offers were Lightning Deals that end once they sell out, so check before counting on them. Shop for the card the way you'd shop for the item it's paying for, because the first discount you see may not be the deepest. Warehouse clubs are a good place to look. Sam's Club advertised up to 25% off gift cards, and BJ's had 18% off a Barnes & Noble card. Costco's gift-card discounts are for members only, though. If you don't belong, judge the deal you can actually get, not the best one you've read about.

Some "gift card deals" don't make the card any cheaper. Instead, the retailer hands you a card as a bonus for buying something else. Walmart offered a $300 gift card with a qualifying iPhone 18 purchase for Black Friday, and Barnes & Noble gave a $10 card for every $100 in gift cards bought. A bonus card doesn't lower what you pay for the item itself. A discounted card trims your bill from the first dollar. A bonus card is only worth counting if you were already planning the purchase and know you'll spend the card. Otherwise it's a reason to spend more, not a saving. Settle the store, the card's price and what you'll buy with it before you buy the card. That's how a gift card actually puts you ahead.

Card-linked cash back cuts the cost of a shopping trip without changing anything in your cart. Banks and card issuers, through programs like Chase Offers, Amex Offers and Bank of America's BankAmeriDeals, run promotions with specific retailers that credit money back on purchases you'd make anyway. The reward comes out of spending you'd already planned, not a new purchase. It lowers the cost of money you're already spending, and it gives you no reason to spend more.

The catch is that it only covers certain stores, and you have to switch it on. Chase says its offers come through partnerships with select merchants, and you need to activate an offer before you make the purchase for it to count. Offers are usually tied to one card, too, so you have to pay with that card. The store you're heading to may not have an offer at all. Checking your banking app before you leave tells you whether the trip will earn anything. That means the app comes out before the card does. Some tools can handle the activating for you. Savewise, a browser extension and app, says its Pro tier automatically activates offers from Chase, SimplyMiles and Rakuten. It also tries to activate Amex offers, though it recommends adding those by hand for guaranteed activation. If you're still shopping this weekend, a quick check in the app before you reach the register is all this kind of cash back asks of you.

Cash back is a bonus on a good price, never a reason to accept a bad one. Money coming back feels good, and that feeling can make it easy to skip the question of whether the price was worth paying in the first place. "If you're not getting a good price on your purchase, earning 3% back doesn't matter," Jason Stauffer, a senior reporter at CNBC Select, said. A refund of a few percent won't turn an overpriced item into a bargain.

The order to follow is simple: judge the price, activate the offer, then pay.

Before you pay any Black Friday price, you can find out whether other people think it's worth paying. Slickdeals is a community site where shoppers post the deals they find, and its millions of members vote and comment on each one. Those votes and comments decide which deals get featured. In effect, you get the judgment of people who have already looked hard at the same offer. Commenters will say so when a posted deal is weaker than it looks, and they often share discount codes that actually work. When an offer comes with a big advertised saving, the comments under it can tell you more than the headline above it. Reading them takes a minute, and the time to do it is before you check out.

Two things in those comments are worth looking for. The first is whether the store advertising the deal is even the right place to buy, since commenters sometimes point to another retailer selling the same item for less. If you trust the first store that promotes an offer, you may pay more than someone who scrolled a few replies further. The second is whether the discount is as big as the store claims. Commenters often mention what the item cost before, which tells you whether it's been this cheap already. With that history in hand, you can hold a dramatic "was" price up against what the item has actually sold for, instead of taking the store's word for it.

On some items, the cheapest version for sale this weekend is one another shopper already sent back. Returned and open-box goods can cost less than the same item new at its Black Friday price. Amazon says shoppers saved more than 25% on average on items from Amazon Resale, its used and returned goods section, last year. Each item is inspected and graded before it's resold. "Like New" means it works perfectly but the packaging may be damaged. The grades step down through "Very Good" and "Good" to "Acceptable," which can mean scratches, dents or missing parts. Best Buy does something similar with open-box items. Its Geek Squad grades them Excellent, Good or Fair, and the price moves with the grade. That makes open-box a better fit for things you're keeping than for gifts, because a beat-up box doesn't matter when the item is for you. The real question isn't whether it costs less. It's whether you trust the grade behind the lower price.

Amazon handles so many returns that some checks slip through. "Because it's such a large operation, things are missed," Zoe Lu, general manager at Helium 10, told CNBC. Amazon's seller programs find new buyers or new homes for more than 300 million items a year. At that volume, a flawed return can land in the resale listings without anyone catching it, and a missed check leaves the risk with you. That risk is worth taking on something you can test the day it arrives, not on something you can't. Read the return terms, too. Both Amazon and Best Buy say open-box and Resale items fall under their regular return policies. Best Buy notes that many open-box items keep the manufacturer's warranty, but it's worth confirming for the specific item.

The new price you're comparing against can also creep up. Amazon's fee changes led 65% of sellers to raise prices in 2024, according to a SmartScout survey cited by CNBC. Some of the gap between a new item and a returned one may come from a higher new price rather than a real bargain on the open-box version. The comparison that counts is the open-box price against the lowest price for a new one anywhere.

A returned item belongs in your cart only when it's the cheapest way to get the thing, not just the cheapest version of it at one store.

Shopping through a cash-back portal adds a second saving on top of the sale price. Click through to a retailer from a site like Rakuten or TopCashback and you earn a percentage back after the Black Friday discount. But that rebate is only worth having on a price that's already the lowest you can find, and a juicy cash-back rate can steer you to the wrong store. Say a TV costs $399 at a store paying 5% back, about $20, while the same set is $299 somewhere else. The cheaper store wins before any money comes back at all. So find the lowest price first, then check whether a portal covers that store.

Cash back can't count as part of the price you pay this weekend, because you don't have it yet. Rakuten says online and in-store purchases show up first as "pending." They typically take three to 14 weeks to be confirmed, a buffer that covers returns, exchanges and other changes to your order. Even then, Rakuten pays out only four times a year, on Feb. 15, May 15, Aug. 15 and Nov. 15. Cash back has to be confirmed before a payment date to make that check, and you need at least $5 confirmed to get paid. Cash back from a Black Friday purchase may not reach you until spring. Until then, it's a balance sitting with the portal, not money in your account. Treat it as a bonus to bank if it shows up, not a number to subtract from the price at the register.

Two shoppers standing side by side in the same aisle can pay different prices for the same item, depending on whether one of them is signed in. Plenty of retailers save some prices for members and app users. Target Circle, Target's free loyalty program, gives members automatic deals and personalized offers in the Target app. So finding the lowest price this weekend depends on which store you're in and on what that store knows about you. The check takes seconds. Before you reach the register, open the store's app or sign in to your account and see whether it offers you a lower price than the one on the shelf. If it doesn't, you've lost a moment. If it does, the number on the tag was never the lowest price the store was willing to charge you.

A members' price is only cheaper once you count what it cost to become a member. Paying to join a program just to grab a small markdown is a bad trade, because you pay the fee before you see any discount. Paid tiers often sell themselves on early access rather than lower prices. Target Circle 360 members got 24 hours of early access to select Black Friday deals. Walmart+ members got Walmart's online "Hot Deal" drops a day before everyone else, and non-members could still buy them the next day while supplies lasted. That gives you a simple rule in the aisle. A free app or a free account passes the test, because access costs nothing and any lower price is a real saving. A paid membership taken out for one weekend of sales usually fails. The fee goes on the bill alongside whatever you buy, and on a modest purchase the discount may never earn it back.

The fee is part of the price, so add it in before you decide the members' rate is a bargain.

A bundle looks like the easiest win in the store: one price covers the thing you came for plus a few extras. That single price is also what makes the deal hard to judge, because you can't see what any one piece costs. A bad bundle can cost you in two ways. Sometimes the package is only slightly cheaper than buying the parts on their own. Other times, part of what you pay goes to accessories you'll never use, which means spending money on things that were never on your list. A bundle only counts as a discount once you've shown that it is one.

The test takes a few minutes on your phone in the aisle. Look up what each item in the bundle costs on its own and add up the prices. It's the one check that tells you whether the package is cheaper than buying just what you need. Keep the comparison like for like, with the same model, the same size and the same extras, because pricing a cheaper lookalike tells you nothing about the bundle on the shelf. The Federal Trade Commission's Guides Against Deceptive Pricing say a "was" price should be a real price the item was regularly offered at, not a number inflated to make a discount look bigger. A bundle's savings claim rests on a reference price too, and here that reference is what the parts cost separately. The difference is that you can look this one up on the spot instead of taking it on trust. If the parts add up to roughly the bundle price, buy only the item you came for and leave the extras behind.

Plenty of shoppers head into this weekend's sales already entitled to a lower price than the one on the tag, without thinking of it as a Black Friday tool. Student, military and teacher discounts can undercut the public sale price, and some go well past an ordinary markdown. HP's Education Program advertises up to 40% off for U.S. students, their parents and teachers. So before you chase the loudest sale sign, figure out which groups you belong to. The best price you can get may depend on who you are, not what day it is.

A student or military rate doesn't win by default. Some are small enough that an ordinary sale beats them, and some take money off an add-on rather than the item itself. Nike's student discount is 10% off most items, and it can't be combined with other promo codes except free shipping. For a student shopping at Nike, any Black Friday markdown deeper than 10% is the better deal. Apple's education pricing includes up to 10% off AppleCare+ coverage for a new Mac or iPad, and a discount on a protection plan is hard to weigh against the price on the laptop's sale tag. Keep in mind that "up to" is a ceiling, so the rate on a given product can be smaller. The sensible move is to put your verified discount price next to the sale price and pay whichever is lower.

A discount has to be proved before it counts, and for a last-minute shopper that proof is the step most likely to be missing. Many retailers run verification through third-party services. Apple uses UNiDAYS, and Nike uses SheerID, which can ask you to upload documents. Nike then emails a single-use code, which works only online, not in Nike stores. Military discounts follow a similar pattern. Nike gives active, reserve, veteran and retired service members 10% off, verified online through SheerID or with a military ID in U.S. stores. Many retailers offer similar rates to teachers, nurses and first responders, so check before assuming students are the only group with a deal.

Sort out your status on your phone before you get in line. At the register, the sale price is the only one on offer.

This trick pays you for doing nothing at checkout. Fill an online cart, get as far as checkout, then leave without paying, and some retailers will email you a discount code to come back. To the store, an abandoned cart is a sale it wants back, and the code is its offer to win you over. On a weekend built around buying fast, the shopper who pauses can end up paying less than the one who clicks "buy" right away.

Nothing about the reward is guaranteed, starting with whether it shows up at all. The tactic depends on the retailer having your email, so you need to be signed in or to have entered your address at checkout. Many retailers do send codes. Electronics retailers and marketplaces like Amazon rarely do, according to research by data firm Decodo reported by ConsumerAffairs. That rules out a lot of the big-ticket items people buy on Black Friday. The size of the discount varies just as much. Decodo found offers ranging from free shipping to as much as 65% off, with fast-fashion brands often sending 10% to 15% within about 12 hours. Waiting has costs of its own. Popular items can sell out, and a price can rise before the code arrives, so screenshot what you saw before you walk away.

A free gift takes nothing off the bill, so it only counts as a saving if you actually want it. Even then, it's only a saving once you've checked that the main item costs no more than it does at other stores. Picture an offer of $100 in free accessories. If you wouldn't have paid even $10 for those accessories, the gift is worth almost nothing to you, whatever value the store puts on it.

Retailers hand out giveaways this week mainly to get people through the door. "Retailers need to offer an attractive incentive for shoppers to visit their store first," retail analyst Bruce Winder told TheStreet. Some of those incentives come down to luck. Michaels is giving away 500 "Countdown to Craftsmas" Advent calendars at each store starting on Black Friday, and only one calendar per store holds a $100 gift card. That's roughly a 1-in-500 shot. If you make the trip for that card, you'll most likely go home without it, after walking past the sale shelves the store wanted you to see.

A freebie can get you in the door, but it doesn't decide whether the trip paid off. TheStreet reports that Neil Saunders, managing director of retail at GlobalData, expects shoppers to want a visit that was worth making, whatever stunt brought them there. Whether a visit was worth making comes down to the price of what you buy. Price the main item against other stores as if no gift came with it. If it costs less, the freebie is a genuine bonus. If it costs more, the gift saved you nothing.

A free gift is the easiest extra to mistake for a saving, because it makes you feel richer even when it saves you nothing.

If the people in the thread have shown that a deal is weaker than it looks, walk past it, however big the advertised saving.

If you always use the same portal out of habit, you could be leaving money on the table, because portals don't all pay the same rate at the same store. Cashback Monitor tracks the rates different portals pay at a given retailer, so you can see who's paying the most before you click. It also shows how a store's best rate has moved over time, which helps you spot a holiday bump. Rates change often, and the gap matters most on big-ticket purchases. That's exactly what a lot of Black Friday shoppers are buying, so any large purchase is worth a quick comparison.

Check the price, then check the portals, and treat whatever comes back as a pleasant surprise rather than part of the deal.

Extras are a way to get you to hand over more at the register, even when each piece looks like a deal.

The bigger risk is that the email talks you into finishing a purchase you'd abandoned for a good reason. Retailers send the code right after you've stopped short of paying, and that timing is what makes it so hard to ignore. A sudden 10% off is a nudge, not a reason. The code works best as a small bonus on something you'd already decided to buy, never as the reason to buy it.

Wait for a code only on things you would have paid full price for anyway, because a cart worth abandoning is still worth abandoning at 10% off.

#5406. Startup Spotlight: An engineer’s search for better, safer baby products led him to launch Birch

Startup Spotlight profiles tech startups in the Pacific Northwest.

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 20, 2026 at 9:41 amNovember 20, 2026 at 9:41 am

A new baby can be the ultimate anxiety trigger: When will she sleep through the night? What if nursing is a challenge. What is that rash?! Given the countless unknowns, the last thing a parent needs are worries about the quality of the baby’s crib or the chemicals in a pacifier.

But when Karthik Gangiredla was preparing for the birth of his first daughter, he and his wife spent hours trying to figure out which baby products were trustworthy.

“We struggled a lot,” Gangiredla said. “We did a lot of research on what was safe, what’s not.”

An engineer with roughly 20 years of experience in supply chains and logistics, including roles at Amazon, Flexport and TikTok, Gangiredla found himself on the consumer side of the retail equation, scrutinizing strollers and bottles.

To spare other parents the same headache, he turned that research into Birch, an online marketplace that offers baby product buying guides and assigns each item a TrustScore. Its scoring system draws on certifications, lab reports and recall databases to help parents assess goods ranging from baby wipes to teething toys.

The site provides information on more than 10,000 items across 110 brands, including manufacturing locations, suppliers, certificate numbers and test reports.

Birch has contracts with brands it has checked out, and serves as their merchant of record, meaning if a customer has issues with a product or wants to return it, Birch handles those steps. It operates fulfillment centers in Los Angeles and New Jersey.

Gangiredla said the startup flips the e-commerce approach of retail giants, focusing on the shoppers’ needs, not those of the merchant. It does not accept ads or sponsored rankings.

If you took away the ad revenue for Amazon or TikTok, “the business wouldn’t exist,” Gangiredla said. “So it’s very difficult for them to approach the problem in a different way.”

The platform also offers a gift registry and tools for tracking fetal development during pregnancy, an infant’s nursing and sleep schedules, and other developmental steps. The tools are free for users.

We caught up with Gangiredla, Birch’s CEO and founder, for this edition of GeekWire’s Startup Spotlight.

In 50 words or less, give us your startup’s elevator pitch

Birch is the trust-first platform for baby and kids products and parenting resources. We research and score products across 50+ safety and quality signals before listing — and stock only what clears the bar — so parents skip the endless research and buy with confidence, from pregnancy through the toddler years.

What problem are you obsessed with solving?

The impossible research burden on new parents. Every purchase feels like a safety decision, the information is scattered and often unverified, and the stakes feel enormous. We’re obsessed with moving the work of figuring out what’s trustworthy off the parent and onto a system that does it rigorously — and then showing our work.

What surprised you after talking to customers?

How universal the trust problem is. We assumed it would track with income or with first-time parents, but our customers span all 50 states and every kind of household — big metros to small towns. And what they consistently want isn’t more options or a lower price; it’s someone to tell them, credibly, what’s actually worth buying.

How has AI changed the way you build your company?

It’s core, not a feature. Our TrustScore engine evaluates thousands of products across dozens of safety and quality signals in ways a human team our size never could, and the same intelligence powers discovery and personalization. It also lets a very lean team operate like a much larger one — and we now license that engine to other baby and kids brands as a product called Juno.

What’s one thing people misunderstand about your startup?

That “curated” means limited or expensive. Curation isn’t about carrying less for its own sake, or about selling premium — it’s about removing the untrustworthy. In our own data, price and trustworthiness barely correlate; some of the highest-scoring products are among the most affordable. Fewer and better, not fewer and pricier.

What’s the toughest decision you’ve made in the past year?

Turning away brands and revenue. When you’re early, every dollar is tempting — but our entire promise is that everything on Birch has earned its place. Saying no to products and partners that didn’t clear the bar, even when the revenue was real, was hard. It’s also the decision that defines what we are.

What’s the one piece of advice you give to other entrepreneurs?

Earn trust before you try to scale it. It’s slower and less glamorous than chasing growth, but trust compounds and shortcuts don’t. And talk to your customers far earlier, and far more often, than feels comfortable.

…a parent’s first instinct, the moment they find out they’re expecting, is to come to Birch — and “did you check the TrustScore?” is just how families talk about buying for their kids.

#5405. Allstate outage: how to file a claim or get roadside help while systems are down

What to do during an Allstate outage, from calling your agent and documenting damage to protecting proof of insurance and avoiding scams that target policyholders

A local Allstate $ALL agent is a human contact who can answer coverage questions, help start a claim and pass details to the company while the app or website is unavailable. Agent contact details usually appear on policy paperwork. That means the office can be reached without logging in to anything.

The declarations page is usually the first place to look. This is the summary sheet that lists a policy's coverages, limits and deductibles, and it often names the servicing agent. Renewal notices, billing statements and welcome letters can carry the same name, phone number and office address.

Older emails, text messages and voicemails from the agency are another record worth checking. A policyholder who saved the agent's number in a phone's contacts already has the quickest route. If an office number turns up through an online search instead, compare it with the printed paperwork before calling.

Policyholders are generally expected to take reasonable steps to stop damage from getting worse, even when they cannot reach their insurer. An app or website being down does not pause that duty. Make temporary fixes, keep every receipt and hold off on permanent repairs until an adjuster has seen the loss.

Standard homeowners policy language spells this out. The common forms published by the Insurance Services Office, which many insurers adapt, list protecting property from further damage among a policyholder's duties after a loss. The same section asks the policyholder to make reasonable and necessary repairs to protect the property. It also asks them to keep an accurate record of what those repairs cost. Individual policies vary, and the wording in your own contract is the one that governs.

A paper or saved copy of your auto insurance ID card lets you prove coverage when Allstate $ALL's app or website won't load. Keep one printed card in the vehicle and one image stored directly on your phone. That way, your proof of insurance does not depend on a live connection.

Drivers in nearly every U.S. state must carry liability coverage. Police can ask to see proof of it during a traffic stop. Drivers involved in a crash typically exchange insurance details at the scene. A registration renewal or a trip to a motor vehicle office can also call for current proof of coverage.

Many drivers now open their ID card inside an insurer's mobile app instead of carrying paper. That method works only when the app can log in and reach the company's servers. If those systems are unavailable, the card may not display at the moment you need it.

Report a loss to Allstate $ALL as soon as you can, even if the app or website is down. Most insurance policies require prompt notice of a claim, and an outage does not pause that duty. A dated record of each attempt to report shows you acted in good faith.

The requirement usually sits in a section of the policy with a title such as "what you must do after a loss" or "duties after loss." Wording varies, but phrases such as "promptly" or "as soon as practicable" are common. Those terms rarely name a fixed number of days. How quickly you must act depends on the policy language and the law in your state.

Read that section before assuming you have time. Some policies set separate, firmer deadlines for specific steps. A homeowners policy may require a signed, sworn proof of loss within a set period after the insurer asks for one. Many policies also include a clause limiting how long you have to sue the insurer over a disputed claim. State law can also affect these windows. Check both the policy text and your state's rules.

Scammers watch for service disruptions and pose as insurance staff to collect payment details, policy numbers or login credentials. During an Allstate $ALL outage, use only phone numbers and web addresses printed on your policy documents or listed on the company's official website. Never give payment information to someone who contacts you first.

An outage hands fraudsters a ready-made story. Policyholders may already expect something to be wrong with their account. A message claiming that a payment failed or a claim stalled can seem plausible as a result.

The pretexts tend to follow a few patterns. A caller may claim to be a claims representative who needs a bank account number to release a payment. A text message may say coverage will lapse unless a premium is "verified" through a link. An email may ask the recipient to log in again on a page that imitates the insurer's site. Each one pushes for quick action and asks for something sensitive.

An insurance policy is a contract, and a contract does not pause because a login page stops loading. When an insurer's app or website goes dark, that alone does not end the coverage a policyholder has paid for. The same goes for the duties the policy places on the customer, from reporting a loss to keeping coverage paid up.

Much of the routine business of insurance has moved to screens. Drivers pull up digital ID cards at traffic stops. Homeowners upload photos of damage, and premiums get paid with a few taps. That convenience can obscure how much still runs through older channels. Claims can be reported by phone. Agents keep offices and phone lines. Premium payments may be possible through an agent or by mail. Complaints can go to a state regulator that sits entirely outside the insurer's systems.

This guide covers what Allstate $ALL policyholders can do during an Allstate outage or any period when the company's digital tools are unavailable.

The most direct way to report a claim when Allstate $ALL's app or website is unavailable is by phone. Use the claims number printed on your insurance ID card or policy documents. A phone report does not depend on the insurer's digital tools.

Start with the paperwork you already have. Auto insurance ID cards typically list a claims contact. Policy packets, declarations pages, renewal notices and billing statements often carry contact details as well. Saved emails from the insurer may include the number too.

Paper records matter here. A policy folder in a desk drawer still works when screens and logins do not.

Gather your information before you dial. The representative will need your policy number to locate your coverage. Have it written down rather than stored only in an app you cannot open.

The basic facts of the loss come next. These include the date and approximate time, the exact location and a plain description of what happened. List what was damaged and whether anyone was hurt.

Auto claims call for more detail about the other parties. Write down the other driver's name, phone number, insurance company and policy number. Add their license plate and the make and model of their vehicle. If police responded, ask for the report number and keep it with your notes. Names and phone numbers of any witnesses belong in the same place.

Home and property claims need a different set of facts. Note the cause if you know it, such as a storm, a burst pipe, a fire or a break-in. Say whether the home is still safe to live in. For a theft, have the police report number ready.

Stick to what you know during the call. If a detail is uncertain, say so instead of guessing. You can add information as the claim moves forward.

Keep a written record of the conversation. Note the date and time of the call and the name of the representative. Ask for a claim or reference number and write it down before hanging up.

Ask what happens next. Find out when an adjuster is expected to contact you. Ask how to send photos and documents if the online portal cannot accept them.

An agent can do several useful things during a disruption. Agency staff can explain what a policy covers and what the deductible is. They can confirm whether a policy is active and help report a new loss. They can also describe the payment methods the office accepts.

There are limits to that role. Claims are typically investigated and settled by adjusters, not by the selling agent. An agent cannot promise a payout, rewrite policy terms or waive a deadline written into the contract. The agency may also depend on the same company systems that are down. Some lookups or document requests may have to wait until those systems return.

Visiting the office in person can help when phone lines are busy. Bring the policy number, a copy of the insurance ID card and any photos of damage. A short written timeline of what happened and when also helps. Ask the staff member to note the visit in the account file.

Write down the name of each person spoken to at the agency, along with the date and time of the conversation. Agency hours vary from office to office. An office may be closed when a loss happens. Outside those hours, the claims number printed on policy documents remains the main route.

Before any cleanup begins, photograph and film all damage to your home, vehicle or belongings. A visual record made right away shows an adjuster the loss as it first looked. It also does not depend on an insurer's app or website being available.

Start wide. Take shots of the whole room, the full exterior wall or all four sides of the car. These show how far the damage extends. Then move in close on each problem area, such as a cracked windshield, a water stain on drywall or a dented door panel.

A slow video walkthrough can capture detail that still photos miss. Narrate as you film. Name the room, the item and what happened. That ties each clip to a specific part of the claim later.

Most smartphones save the date and time in each photo's file data. Keep the original files rather than edited or cropped versions. Back them up to a computer, a cloud account or an email to yourself. That way the record survives if the phone is lost or damaged.

After a car accident, document the scene as well as the vehicles. Useful images include the positions of the cars, road conditions, traffic signs, the other driver's license plate and any visible injuries. Write down the other driver's name, insurer and policy number. Add contact details for any witnesses. If police respond, note the officer's name and the report number.

For damage at home, build a written list of affected items as you photograph them. Include a description, the approximate age and the brand or model where known. Note where in the home each item was. Receipts, bank or card statements, product manuals and older photos of the items can help support their value.

Where it is safe, keep damaged items until an adjuster has inspected them or said they can go. Discarding a ruined appliance or a soaked rug too early can leave a claim with less proof. Spoiled food and anything that poses a health risk may need to go sooner. Photograph those items before disposal.

Store every photo, video and note in a single folder. When the app or claims website works again, or when you reach a representative by phone, the evidence is ready to share.

The duty has a practical side. Many homeowners policies exclude loss caused by neglect, meaning a failure to use all reasonable means to save and preserve property at and after a loss. A small roof leak left open for days can spread to drywall, flooring and insulation. An insurer may then treat that later damage as preventable.

Typical temporary measures are modest. They include covering a damaged roof with a tarp, boarding up a broken window or shutting off the main water valve after a burst pipe. Moving furniture and electronics away from standing water also counts. So does running fans or a dehumidifier to start drying out a wet room.

For a vehicle, the same logic applies on a smaller scale. Standard personal auto policies carry a similar duty to take reasonable steps after a loss to protect the covered vehicle from further loss. Taping plastic sheeting over a shattered window keeps rain out of the interior. Parking a car with a coolant leak or a damaged tire can prevent engine or wheel damage that the original accident did not cause.

Safety comes before any of this. Do not climb onto a wet or storm-damaged roof. Do not walk through standing water near live electrical outlets. For hazardous work, a licensed contractor or emergency water-mitigation company can handle the job instead.

Keep the line between temporary and permanent work clear. Replacing a whole roof or tearing out cabinets before an adjuster inspects can make the claim harder to verify. Save invoices, receipts and payment records for every emergency purchase, from tarps and plywood to a contractor's call-out fee. Note the date of each step as well. A clear timeline is easier to present once the claim is reported.

If damage forces you out of your home, save every receipt for the extra costs of living somewhere else. Additional living expense coverage, often called loss of use, may reimburse those costs. It pays only if your policy includes it, and usually only for spending above your normal budget.

This coverage is common in homeowners and renters policies. Standard homeowners forms usually list it as Coverage D, loss of use. Your declarations page shows whether you have it and what limit applies. Read that page before assuming any expense will be paid.

The coverage typically applies when a covered loss, such as a fire or a burst pipe, makes the home unfit to live in. A loss the policy excludes generally won't trigger it. Flood damage under a standard homeowners policy is one example.

Reimbursement is generally based on the increase in your costs, not the full amount you spend. Mortgage or rent payments usually continue after a loss. A hotel bill on top of them is typically an added cost. Meals work differently. If your household normally spends a set amount on groceries, the claim usually covers the difference between that and what you now spend eating out.

That makes proof of your normal spending useful. Bank statements or past grocery receipts can show your typical monthly costs before the loss.

Keep receipts for hotel stays or short-term rentals, restaurant meals, laundry services and pet boarding. Save records of extra fuel or mileage if a temporary address lengthens your commute. Storage unit fees and the cost of moving into temporary housing also belong in the file.

Photograph each paper receipt as soon as you get it. Thermal receipt paper fades over time. Store the images in email or a cloud folder that doesn't depend on the insurer's app or website. A simple log with the date, amount, vendor and reason for each expense makes the claim easier to review.

Auto policies handle this separately. Rental reimbursement coverage is an optional add-on that may pay for a rental car while a covered vehicle is being repaired. If your auto declarations page doesn't list it, rental costs are generally your own.

Before committing to a large or long-term expense, such as a monthly lease, confirm with your agent or adjuster that it falls within your coverage. A written approval, even a short email, gives you a record to point to if the expense is questioned later.

A screenshot avoids that problem. Save the image to the phone's photo library or files folder. From there, it opens without an internet connection. A PDF downloaded from an online account works the same way. Zoom $ZM in on the saved copy to confirm that the policy number and dates are readable.

A printed card serves as the backup to the backup. Phones run out of battery, crack and get left at home. A paper card in the glovebox stays with the car no matter who is driving it. ID cards usually list the specific vehicle they cover. Households with more than one insured vehicle need a card for each car.

Insurance ID cards show effective and expiration dates. A card from an earlier policy term does not prove current coverage. Replace printed and saved copies each time the policy renews or a vehicle is added or removed.

Save the declarations page as well. It lists the coverages, limits, deductibles, drivers and vehicles on the policy. A stored PDF of it puts the policy details within reach when you report a claim or answer questions from another driver's insurer.

Rules on whether police and motor vehicle agencies accept electronic proof of insurance differ from state to state. A paper copy covers situations where a digital image is not accepted. Your state's motor vehicle agency can confirm the rules that apply where you drive.

If an outage stops you from paying a premium online, write down every attempt and keep proof of it. Then read your policy's grace period and cancellation language. Those terms, not the status of an app or website, decide what happens to a late payment.

A useful record is simple. Note the date and time of each try, the payment method you used and what happened. If a payment page shows an error message, take a screenshot that captures the date and time on your device. If a payment goes through by any route, save the confirmation number, receipt email or bank reference.

Check your bank or card statement before trying again. A payment that appeared to fail may still have been processed. A second attempt could then produce a duplicate charge. Policyholders enrolled in automatic payments should confirm that the scheduled withdrawal left their account on the expected date.

A local Allstate $ALL agent's office may be able to accept a payment or explain other options while the online portal is down. Billing statements and policy paperwork generally list a mailing address for checks. If you mail a payment, use a service that documents the mailing date, such as certified mail through the U.S. Postal Service. Keep a copy of the check and the mailing receipt.

Grace period terms vary by policy, by type of coverage and by state. Some policies allow a window after the due date, and its length is not uniform. Do not assume one applies to your policy or matches the terms of an earlier policy. The billing and cancellation sections of the policy, along with any billing notice, set out the actual rules.

State insurance laws generally require an insurer to send written notice before canceling a policy for nonpayment. The notice rules, including how far in advance it must arrive, differ from state to state. A cancellation notice typically names a date by which payment must be received to keep coverage in force. Read any such notice closely if one arrives during or after a service disruption.

A lapse can carry consequences beyond the policy itself. Most states require drivers to carry auto liability insurance, and a gap in coverage can trigger state penalties. Mortgage lenders and auto lenders often require continuous coverage. If a borrower's policy lapses, a lender may buy coverage on the borrower's behalf, usually at a higher cost.

The payment log matters if a billing dispute arises later. Dated records of on-time attempts through more than one channel give a policyholder something concrete to show the insurer.

Late notice can put a claim at risk. Courts in many states apply what is known as the notice-prejudice rule. Under it, an insurer generally must show that a delay harmed its ability to investigate before denying a claim for lateness. Not every state follows that rule, and it may not cover every type of policy. Reporting early keeps the question from arising.

If digital channels fail, use another route and document it. Write down the date, time, method and outcome of every attempt, including calls that went unanswered. Save screenshots of error messages showing the app or site was unavailable. These records help show that the delay did not start with you.

Written notice adds a second layer of proof. An email to your agent carries its own timestamp, and a dated letter serves the same purpose. Include your policy number, the date and location of the loss and a short description. Sending a letter by USPS Certified Mail with a return receipt gives you proof of delivery.

Some losses carry reporting duties outside the insurer. Auto policies commonly require you to notify police after a vehicle theft. Uninsured motorist coverage for a hit-and-run often requires a police report as well. File those reports promptly, and keep each report number with your claim records.

If Allstate $ALL does not respond to a claim, a payment problem or a coverage question within a reasonable time, a policyholder can file a complaint with their state's insurance regulator. Every state runs an office that accepts consumer complaints about insurers.

Insurance in the U.S. is regulated mainly at the state level rather than by a single federal agency. Congress affirmed that arrangement in the McCarran-Ferguson Act, passed in 1945. The agency that oversees an Allstate policy therefore depends on the state where the policy was issued. The location of the company's headquarters does not decide it.

The office goes by different names. Many states call it the department of insurance. Others use a division of insurance or an insurance commissioner's office. In New York, insurance oversight sits with the Department of Financial Services. The National Association of Insurance Commissioners keeps a directory of state regulators on its website. The official state government site will also list the correct agency.

A complaint makes the most sense after direct contact has failed. That means the policyholder has already tried the claims line, the local agent or written correspondence. It also means they have not received an answer or a fair resolution. Regulators generally expect consumers to give the insurer a chance to fix the problem first.

A useful complaint is specific. It should include the policy number and the claim number, if one exists. It should also name anyone the policyholder spoke with and give a timeline of each contact attempt. Copies of letters, emails, photos and receipts help a reviewer see what happened. A clear statement of the outcome the policyholder wants also helps the review.

Most state departments accept complaints through an online form. Many also take them by mail or phone. After a complaint arrives, the department typically forwards it to the insurer and asks for a written response. A reviewer then checks whether the company followed the policy terms and state law.

A regulator does not act as the policyholder's lawyer. It usually cannot settle a factual dispute over how much a claim is worth. Complaint records still serve a purpose beyond the individual case. State regulators use them to spot patterns in how an insurer treats customers. Recurring problems can lead to a formal market conduct examination of the company.

Caller ID offers little protection. Phone numbers can be spoofed to display a legitimate company name or a familiar area code. Email sender names can be faked the same way. A display name that matches the insurer is not proof the message came from it.

The safer move is to end the contact and start a new one yourself. Hang up or close the message. Then dial the number on your ID card, declarations page or a past bill. A local agent you already work with is another route. If the original request was genuine, someone on that verified line can confirm it.

Links in unexpected texts and emails call for the same caution. Typing the insurer's address directly into a browser avoids lookalike domains that differ by a single letter or an added word. Passwords and one-time security codes should never go to anyone who calls or writes asking for them.

Suspected scams can be reported. The Federal Trade Commission collects fraud reports from consumers. The National Insurance Crime Bureau accepts tips about insurance fraud. Many state insurance departments also run fraud units that take reports of people impersonating insurers.

Anyone who already shared card or bank details should contact the bank or card issuer right away to flag the account. Keep a copy of the suspicious message, along with the number or address it came from.

#5404. Stop Using AI as an Excuse for Layoffs. Here’s How to Use AI to Retain Talent Instead

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

How to use AI to make your team more capable, not smaller.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

When a company announces layoffs and points to AI, I always want to know what happened first. Did the technology fundamentally change how work gets done, or did leadership already need to reduce costs and AI became a convenient explanation?

There is a meaningful difference. AI can automate tasks, accelerate workflows and change the skills a company needs. But AI does not walk into a boardroom and decide how many people should remain employed. Leaders decide what happens to the capacity the technology creates.

That distinction matters because employees are watching. If every AI announcement is followed by layoffs, people quickly learn that greater efficiency puts their jobs at risk and they have little reason to embrace the tools leadership wants them to use.

There is another way to implement AI. Start by asking how it can make your people more capable.

I learned this lesson long before the current AI boom. When we were building Amazon Web Services, talented engineers were spending too much time provisioning servers, configuring storage and handling infrastructure before they could get to the work they were actually there to do. By removing that friction, we gave developers more capacity to build, experiment and solve customer problems.

I saw the same principle years later with a junior attorney who spent hours researching and formatting before reaching the work that required her judgment. Generative AI could produce a first draft in minutes, giving her more time to refine the facts and shape the narrative for the client’s best outcome.

That is the opportunity leaders should look for with AI. Before calculating how many positions an efficiency gain could eliminate, ask what your people could accomplish if repetitive work stopped consuming so much of their day.

Suppose AI gives a team back 10 or 20% of its capacity. What happens to that time?

It could be the customer follow-up that keeps getting postponed, an improvement sitting in the backlog or a relationship that needs more attention. Those opportunities already exist inside most businesses. The problem is that people have been too busy with repetitive work to pursue them.

I saw this with a team of customer service agents who spent a significant portion of their day filling out forms and navigating cumbersome systems. An AI tool automated part of that process and gave them roughly an hour back each day.

Leadership could have used that hour to justify a smaller team. Instead, employees spent more time connecting with customers, strengthening relationships and solving more complex problems. AI removed work they disliked and created room for work where they could contribute more.

Retaining talent requires planning for people at the beginning of an AI initiative rather than after deployment. If leaders automate first and ask what happens to employees later, the priority is already clear.

Before introducing AI, divide the work into three categories. Some tasks contain little meaningful judgment and can be automated. Others can be accelerated by AI while still requiring human judgment. A third group should remain primarily human because relationships, creativity or judgment create the value. Then make the next decision before deploying anything. Where will the recovered capacity go?

That could mean moving people toward customer relationships, product development, higher-level analysis or other work that contributes more directly to growth. The destination will vary by organization, but leaders should know where they want people to go before technology begins changing their roles.

How you introduce AI also shapes whether employees embrace or resist it. If the first message people hear is that a tool will save 40% of their time, they may immediately wonder what leadership plans to do with that 40%.

Tell employees which frustrating work you want to reduce. Show them what they will have more time to accomplish. Explain how their roles can become more valuable as AI handles repetitive tasks.

Then demonstrate that commitment through what happens next. If employees see recovered time consistently reinvested into better work, stronger skills and new opportunities, AI starts to look like a tool they can use rather than a threat they need to survive.

Leaders can begin before buying another AI tool. Take one team and map how AI could change its work, then answer these four questions together before deployment.

1. What work should disappear? Break roles into individual tasks and identify repetitive work that consumes time without requiring significant human judgment. Focus first on removing friction rather than removing positions.

2. What human capability should grow? For every task AI can automate or accelerate, identify what employees could do with the recovered time. Look for work involving customers, relationships, creativity, problem-solving or judgment.

3. Where will the recovered capacity go? Give those hours a destination before deployment. If AI saves a team eight hours each week, decide whether those hours will go toward customer service, innovation, new revenue opportunities or another measurable priority.

4. What will you tell employees? Explain what AI will take off their plates and what you want them doing more of as a result. Managers should be able to describe that future clearly before asking employees to adopt the technology.

AI will change jobs, and some roles will change significantly as companies redesign how work gets done. But leaders still control a critical decision about what they do with the capacity AI creates.

Before treating efficiency as a reason to reduce headcount, ask what your people could accomplish with the time they get back. The companies that answer that question first have an opportunity to use AI for something far more valuable than cutting costs. They can use it to build a more capable workforce.

When a company announces layoffs and points to AI, I always want to know what happened first. Did the technology fundamentally change how work gets done, or did leadership already need to reduce costs and AI became a convenient explanation?

There is a meaningful difference. AI can automate tasks, accelerate workflows and change the skills a company needs. But AI does not walk into a boardroom and decide how many people should remain employed. Leaders decide what happens to the capacity the technology creates.

That distinction matters because employees are watching. If every AI announcement is followed by layoffs, people quickly learn that greater efficiency puts their jobs at risk and they have little reason to embrace the tools leadership wants them to use.

#5403. Microsoft ‘To Do’ users make a big to-do over popular task app’s pending retirement

by Todd Bishop on Nov 20, 2026 at 2:06 pmNovember 20, 2026 at 2:08 pm

Microsoft acquired the popular Wunderlist app in 2015, shut it down in 2020 and told its loyal users that Microsoft To Do would be their new home. Now it’s asking them to switch again.

Microsoft plans to retire the To Do apps on June 30, 2027, moving personal task management for work and school accounts into Planner, its team project-management app. Microsoft disclosed the change Wednesday in a long Planner blog post amid the company’s Ignite announcements, and Windows Latest flagged the change later that day.

The reaction was swift and mostly unhappy. Tom Warren of The Verge summed it up on X: “Microsoft is killing its great tasks app in favor of its worse tasks app.”

That’s not entirely fair to Planner, which is built for a different job. But it captures the gripe: To Do was simple, free and worked across Windows, Mac, iOS, Android and the web, and nothing Microsoft is offering replaces all of that.

For work and school accounts, Microsoft says Planner “will be the destination for managing personal work tasks,” but “existing To Do tasks and lists will not migrate to Planner.” It says it will offer a way to export To Do data before the app shuts down.

Tony Redmond of Office365itpros, who tracks Microsoft 365 closely, cataloged the gaps: no file attachments on private Planner tasks, no equivalent for To Do’s list groups, no transfer of shared-list membership, assignments or permissions, and no native Planner apps for Windows or Mac.

He also noted the irony that Outlook’s old Exchange-based tasks will outlive To Do.

Why Microsoft is doing it: The company said putting individual and shared work on the same foundation lets it deliver more consistent features, and lets people connect their own tasks to Copilot and other AI agents. A new Planner agent, available with a Copilot add-on license, can take on tasks and generate status reports.

The Register’s Richard Speed put it less charitably, saying Microsoft had slipped the news into “this week’s Ignite AI puffery.”

Users weigh in: Brad Silverberg, the former Microsoft executive who led Windows 95 development and later became a Seattle venture investor, posted on X that he has used To Do daily, and Wunderlist before it.

“Very disappointed now,” he wrote, adding that he’s looking at TickTick and Todoist.

Similar posts piled up on LinkedIn from Microsoft 365 consultants and everyday users, some of them describing Planner as clunky by comparison.

Patrick Husting, a Seattle-area entrepreneur and software developer whose Ghostwriter add-in brought AI to Microsoft Office before Microsoft announced Microsoft 365 Copilot, offered on LinkedIn to maintain To Do for Microsoft for free.

Rivals smell an opportunity: Competitors wasted no time. TickTick posted a migration guide for To Do refugees. Todoist CEO Amir Salihefendic wrote on LinkedIn that the shutdown was “pretty unexpected” and pointed out that his app has outlasted competitors for 20 years.

The most pointed pitch came from Superlist, which called itself “the natural successor” and said it already has a tool for importing To Do lists. Wunderlist founder Christian Reber started the company in 2020.

Reber and his co-founders sold Wunderlist’s parent company, 6Wunderkinder, to Microsoft in 2015 for a reported $100 million to $200 million. In 2019, as Microsoft prepared to shut the app down, he publicly asked Satya Nadella to sell it back. Microsoft kept it, then retired it in favor of To Do.

Now some of those former Wunderlist users may end up back with the people who built it.

#5402. Should You Run Your Own AI or Pay a Provider? Here’s How to Decide.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Open-weight models finally give businesses a real choice between running AI on their own servers or renting it from the cloud.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

I’m an AI engineer and I’m currently building ChatMakr, an AI-powered platform that creates multi-agent chatbots in seconds, powered by open-weight models. I also spent time at a consulting firm focused on innovation financing, where I talked with hundreds of Parisian entrepreneurs, and this exact question — run it yourself or rent it from someone else — came up constantly. Open-weight models have made that question sharper than ever, so here’s how to actually think through it.

An open-weight model is a model whose trained parameters are published for anyone to download and run, without necessarily sharing the code or data used to train it. As the Open Source Initiative defines it, “Open Weights refer to the final weights and biases of a trained neural network.” You get the finished brain, not the recipe that built it. That distinction is exactly why open-weight models matter for this decision: because you can download the weights, you’re free to run them on your own hardware, on a cloud provider’s hardware or switch between the two, instead of being locked into one company’s API.

Self-hosting means running that open-weight model on infrastructure you control, whether that’s a GPU server sitting in your own office or a rented GPU virtual machine you fully manage. You pick the hardware, you install the software and you’re responsible for keeping it running.

Cloud means renting inference from a provider instead, whether that’s a managed endpoint hosting an open-weight model for you or a closed API you call over the internet. But cloud isn’t one single choice, because where that provider is headquartered changes what legal system governs your data. A U.S. cloud provider, even one running a data center inside the EU, remains bound by the CLOUD Act.

Here’s how it actually plays out. Below, I’ll call the winner between self-host and cloud on six specific fronts.

Self-hosting looks expensive on paper because you’re paying for a GPU whether you use it or not, but at high enough volume that fixed cost stops mattering. Cloudzy’s cost analysis explains that “self-hosting an open-weight model on a GPU VPS can beat a frontier API at high, sustained volume with good GPU utilization.” The catch is that most businesses never generate that kind of steady, maxed-out traffic. For anyone below that threshold, cloud wins on cost.

Running your own GPUs doesn’t just cost hardware money, it costs people, and that line item is easy to underestimate. Activepieces breaks down the real total cost of ownership and finds that “the payroll for these positions often exceeds the annual budget for the H100 GPUs they manage.” The engineers who keep a self-hosted stack alive frequently cost more than the chips they’re maintaining. Cloud wins here, because the provider absorbs that staffing burden for you.

For businesses handling sensitive or regulated data, who can legally compel access to your information matters as much as who can technically breach it. MassiveGRID lays out the jurisdiction problem plainly: “a U.S.-headquartered provider operating servers in the EU is still subject to the CLOUD Act,” while “a provider incorporated and operating entirely within the EU provides stronger protection against extraterritorial data access requests.” Self-hosting on your own hardware or choosing an EU-only cloud provider closes off that exposure entirely. Self-hosting, or EU cloud specifically, wins on legal exposure.

Demand for AI products rarely arrives in a straight line, and that’s where renting infrastructure pays off. Buzzclan defines the core benefit of cloud elasticity as “the ability to automatically adjust infrastructure capacity based on demand, helping businesses maintain performance without overprovisioning.” A self-hosted GPU server can’t grow on demand during a traffic spike or shrink back down when things go quiet, it just sits at whatever size you bought it at. Cloud wins on scalability.

Open-weight models exist precisely because businesses want to shape the model itself, not just prompt around its limits. A closed cloud API gives you a fixed model behind a fixed interface. Self-hosting wins on customization.

For a business selling into enterprise customers, a provider’s paperwork can matter as much as its performance. Google Cloud explains what its SOC 2 report actually verifies: “the SOC 2 reports are generated by an objective third party attesting to a set of assertions made by Google Cloud about its controls that are in place to protect customer data.” Building that same audited trail yourself, on your own servers, takes real time and specialized staff most startups don’t have. Cloud wins on compliance.

There’s no single winner here, and that’s the actual takeaway. Open-weight models made this a genuine choice instead of a forced one: The same model can run in a rented data center or on a box you own, and the right answer depends on which of these six factors matters most to your business right now.

If you’re regulated or handling sensitive data, lean self-host or EU cloud. If you’re scaling unpredictably or don’t want to hire an infrastructure team, lean cloud. Most businesses will end up doing both — cloud for the unpredictable parts, self-hosting for the parts that need full control — and that’s not indecision; it’s just matching the infrastructure to the actual argument that matters most in each case.

I’m an AI engineer and I’m currently building ChatMakr, an AI-powered platform that creates multi-agent chatbots in seconds, powered by open-weight models. I also spent time at a consulting firm focused on innovation financing, where I talked with hundreds of Parisian entrepreneurs, and this exact question — run it yourself or rent it from someone else — came up constantly. Open-weight models have made that question sharper than ever, so here’s how to actually think through it.

An open-weight model is a model whose trained parameters are published for anyone to download and run, without necessarily sharing the code or data used to train it. As the Open Source Initiative defines it, “Open Weights refer to the final weights and biases of a trained neural network.” You get the finished brain, not the recipe that built it. That distinction is exactly why open-weight models matter for this decision: because you can download the weights, you’re free to run them on your own hardware, on a cloud provider’s hardware or switch between the two, instead of being locked into one company’s API.

Self-hosting means running that open-weight model on infrastructure you control, whether that’s a GPU server sitting in your own office or a rented GPU virtual machine you fully manage. You pick the hardware, you install the software and you’re responsible for keeping it running.

#5401. Dua Lipa defined internet cool. In a $44 billion creator economy, her successor may be harder to buy

Being the internet’s cool girl takes surprising work for someone who’s supposed to make it look effortless. She knows about the hole-in-the-wall restaurant before the line wraps around the block, has a vacation wardrobe worth taking notes on, and somehow finds time to read the book everyone will be talking about in six months.

Few have mastered that balancing act as well as Dua Lipa. The Grammy-winning pop star has become as much an inspiration for where to vacation, what to read, and where to eat as for what to listen to.

She interviews authors like Margaret Atwood for her book club, shares cultural recommendations through her lifestyle platform, Service95, and is a fixture in the fashion world.

But after years of celebrities turning their personalities into businesses and influencers making nearly every aspect of their lives shoppable, the economics of being cool may be changing. Being everywhere may no longer make someone worth following, which poses a slight problem for an industry that makes money off visibility.

U.S. spending on creator advertising is expected to reach $44 billion this year, more than triple the $13.9 billion spent in 2021, according to the Interactive Advertising Bureau. But even as brands pour more money into the creator economy, younger consumers are growing weary of its biggest stars.

A July survey of 13- to 39-year-olds from youth research firm YPulse found that 62% are tired of seeing the same big names everywhere, while 73% trust smaller creators more than big influencers.

“You can pay for attention, but you can’t buy cultural credibility or this idea of being cool,” Izzy Farmiloe, global head of strategy and growth at Dazed Studio, the agency arm of youth culture and fashion publisher Dazed Media, told Fortune.

Long before Instagram gave celebrities a place to document their breakfast, much of the fascination with the cool girl came from how little the public knew about her.

In a November essay for his newsletter, Considered Chaos, brand strategist Eugene Healey explained how each generation’s cool girl was shaped by the media of her time. Kate Moss had fashion magazines, the Olsen twins had the paparazzi, and Alexa Chung had fashion blogs and street-style photographers.

Social media brought audiences closer to the women they admired, making relatability an asset for personalities like Emma Chamberlain. As algorithms began serving up content based on people’s interests rather than simply who they followed, celebrities also had more reason to venture beyond the industries that made them famous.

“Dua Lipa was made for the feed,” Healey wrote.

Her friendship with designer Simon Porte Jacquemus might draw in fashion enthusiasts, while her book club could introduce her to someone who has never listened to Future Nostalgia. Each new audience offers another opportunity to make money beyond selling records and concert tickets.

It’s a business model that has become increasingly familiar, with celebrities launching beauty brands, starting newsletters, and inviting followers into their kitchens. Somewhere along the way, having a favorite lip gloss became an opportunity to launch a cosmetics company.

The trouble with making a living off being cool is that the more people see someone being paid to recommend things, the harder it becomes to tell what she actually likes. Even the seemingly casual Instagram photo dump, filled with blurry pictures and half-eaten meals, can be as carefully curated as the polished posts it was meant to replace.

For Jenna Drenten, a marketing professor at Loyola University Chicago, the problem lies in the very nature of an influencer’s job. “They are expected to sell what is popular, but also expected to discover what’s new,” Drenten told Fortune.

Drenten pointed to BookTok, where recommending a novel outside the usual bestseller rotation can set a creator apart. If enough people take her advice, however, the book becomes just another BookTok sensation, losing some of the very appeal that made it worth recommending in the first place.

Brands risk falling into the same trap. Farmiloe has seen companies chase the same trends and hire the same talent in their pursuit of relevance, spending money only to end up looking more like one another.

“I actually think silence can often be a stronger strategy now,” Farmiloe said.

Trying too hard to look polished may also backfire for brands, especially as artificial intelligence makes it easier to produce everything from flawless images to cultural recommendations. “To sort of show mistakes is a way of proving that a human has made something,” Farmiloe said, adding that even typos have become chic.

Healey identified three potential successors to the Dua Lipa era: the obsessive, who knows a particular subject inside and out; the ghost, whose reputation spreads without constantly posting; and the host, who brings people together in real life.

He argued that the three share expertise and charisma that are hard to fake at a moment when faking has never been easier. If the next dominant medium is an AI model that can summarize the world’s knowledge on demand, Healey wrote, cool becomes whatever can’t be summarized.

For brands accustomed to measuring influence in followers, likes, and views, the next cool girl may be much harder to price. Drenten sees growing appeal in people who can offer something beyond a product recommendation, whether it’s a longtime librarian who can introduce readers to literature they might never have discovered on their own or someone who brings strangers together outside the confines of their carefully curated feeds.

As going out becomes increasingly expensive, Farmiloe sees an opportunity for brands to help create those experiences. She pointed to Reference Point, a London library, bookshop, and bar that doubles as a gathering place for chess, poetry, and jazz.

Rather than paying someone to talk about a brand, companies could give people a place to spend time together.

“Instead of just getting noticed, how do you get people to care or actually like engage or spend time with your brand?” Farmiloe said.

Tatiana Sataua is a News Fellow at Fortune covering business, technology, AI, and consumer culture.
