#5399. Microsoft’s final Outlook outage report details testing gaps and safeguards that backfired

by Todd Bishop on Nov 21, 2026 at 9:31 amNovember 21, 2026 at 9:50 am

The bug behind last week’s global Microsoft 365 outage struck only newer, more powerful servers in a key part of Microsoft’s network. That’s because it created a kind of traffic jam inside each server, and the more work a machine tried to do at once, the worse the jam got. The newer servers are built to do more at once, so they’re the ones that seized up.

One reason Microsoft didn’t catch it in advance: it was testing on older servers.

“Our testing did not adequately represent the combination of hardware and traffic mix encountered during this incident,” the company acknowledged in its final report, released Friday evening, a week after resolving the outage that crippled Outlook and cut off email for people around the world.

Testing that more closely replicates the company’s production environment is one of 13 next steps in the report — measures the company says it will take to keep it from happening again. The list is also aimed at reassuring the businesses that rely on Microsoft for email and collaboration, after CEO Satya Nadella acknowledged at the company’s Ignite conference this week that it has work to do on resilience.

Many of the other steps identified in the report go after a bigger problem: during the incident, the safeguards meant to contain the failure spread it around the world instead.

What set it off: As detailed in Microsoft’s preliminary report last weekend, the bug at the center of the outage had been sitting dormant since July, when Microsoft started rolling out the software update that introduced it. For more than three months, it caused no problems.

The bug affected the servers that make up what Microsoft calls its network gateway, a front door that connects people to Outlook email and other Microsoft 365 services. The flaw came from a Windows update used only on those servers. Standard versions of Windows weren’t affected.

So what was the bug? Microsoft’s final report gives a partial answer, saying it came from a change to how the gateway servers handle incoming connections.

Under heavy load, it turned out, the Windows process that sets up those connections bogged down, with tasks stuck waiting on each other until the servers ran out of computing power and memory and stopped responding.

The final report doesn’t say what the July update was meant to fix. But it does lay out three conditions that finally set the bug off. Without the bug, even all three together would have been routine, the report says.

First, nearly 14% of the gateway’s server capacity was already offline that day for routine software updates. That’s normally not a problem, because Microsoft keeps enough spare capacity to absorb it. But it meant fewer servers were available to carry the load.

That’s a different explanation from the preliminary report, which blamed the missing capacity on an unrelated problem.

Second, all of Microsoft Teams’ traffic landed on those same servers. Teams normally runs through a separate gateway of its own. About 15 hours before the outage, a routing glitch on that Teams gateway in Microsoft’s US East region set off an automatic switch that moved all Teams traffic worldwide onto the servers that handle email.

Third, the U.S. workday got going. Widespread failures began around 8 a.m. Pacific, as traffic in North America climbed toward its daily peak.

How it spread: As servers stopped responding, Microsoft’s systems automatically moved their traffic to healthy servers nearby, which had the same bug and buckled under the extra load. At the low point, more than 80% of the gateway’s servers in North America were unresponsive.

The system then shifted traffic to other regions, spreading the problem further.

“Within about two hours of the broad failures that began in North America, servers in every region were affected globally,” the report says.

The preliminary report had blamed that spread partly on “a separate issue.” The final report doesn’t repeat or explain that phrase. Instead, its findings say the way Microsoft distributes traffic “can cascade failures to other regions.”

Once the servers went down, getting them back up was its own problem. As servers came back online, they were swamped by pent-up demand and froze again, a pattern engineers call a “thundering herd.” Microsoft says it will ease traffic back onto recovering servers gradually. That fix doesn’t have a date yet.

The fixes: To keep a failure from spreading again, Microsoft says it will change how its systems shift traffic between regions, so a problem in one part of the world stays there.

It also plans to split up the servers that handle email, so a surge from another service like Teams can’t take them down. And Teams will switch over only in the region that has the problem, not worldwide.

Some of the fixes are due by the end of the year, others by the end of March. Several don’t have a date yet.

Microsoft says its first notice to customers went out about 20 minutes after the outage took hold, and it plans to shorten that by the end of the year. No business email was lost, according to the report, though some delayed messages to consumer mailboxes that had been inactive for more than 30 days bounced back to senders.

The report also confirms what Microsoft said the day after the outage began: it wasn’t hackers, and it wasn’t AI. “This incident was confirmed not to be caused by a cyberattack, and we found no evidence of malicious activity,” it says. “This change was not caused by AI tooling.”

The new testing is supposed to be in place by the end of March, according to the final report. This time, the company says, the machines in the lab will actually match the ones running the service in production.

#5398. Hackers breach Air Force cloud as cyberattacks hit the CIA, FBI and Pentagon

Reuters tracked 2026 intrusions at the Air Force, CIA, FBI, Pentagon and more. Five incidents, and who did it is still unclear.

A government hack is often pictured as one dramatic event, but in 2026 break-ins at U.S. agencies became public one after another. President Trump confirmed in a Fox News interview on Nov. 21 that hackers had broken into an FBI database, according to CNBC, and within days the public learned of a breach at an intelligence agency as well. Each new disclosure arrived before the last one had been explained. The targets also went beyond spy and military agencies to departments that most people rarely connect with national security.

What ties these breaches together is not a single attacker but how little is known about what the intruders took. No one has spelled out exactly what they got at the intelligence agency, according to the Honolulu Star-Advertiser, or which records they removed from the FBI database. Justin Sherman, a senior associate at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, says no database hack should be waved off as routine because each one connects to others, according to TIME. A breach in 2026 is best judged by what the intruders could reach, not by a confirmed count of stolen files.

Reuters lists the major cyber intrusions of 2026 into U.S. government agencies and other targets. Intruders got into the Air Force's main cloud platform and into a research tool that the CIA shares with the country's top intelligence office, while other attackers went after dozens of commercial ships. What each intruder could reach shows where the real exposure lies, from weapons data and intelligence tools to police records, personnel files and shipping.

Hackers who broke into Cloud One, the Air Force's flagship computing platform, got into the part of the system that manages the entire platform rather than a single application. They reached its control plane by exploiting a software flaw, according to TNW. From there, the intruders potentially exposed aircraft and radar data, along with data from a munitions system used at more than 200 sites.

Getting into the controls does not prove that anyone read the data behind them. No one has shown that the intruders looked at any aircraft or parts records, or publicly identified who got in. U.S. Cyber Command is assessing the damage. The Air Force said in a statement to Reuters that it "does not comment on the security posture, vulnerabilities or operational status of specific networks and systems."

Whether or not the hackers took anything, the Air Force has already lost the use of its flagship cloud for new work. The service's plan to shift its back-office programs onto the platform is on hold, and the software already hosted there can no longer receive updates.

A breach at an intelligence agency makes most people picture stolen secrets, but these hackers got into the tool the agencies use to read the open world. They accessed the open-source scanning system of the CIA and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, which scans unclassified, publicly available material.

The only public reassurance is narrow. The Office of the Director of National Intelligence said there were "no disruptions to critical capabilities or classified systems." That statement rules out breakage, not entry.

Early signs point to possible Chinese involvement, but no account of how the intruders got in has been made public, so China remains a suspicion rather than a confirmed finding.

The hackers reached a tool two intelligence agencies use, and who did it is still unsettled.

At the Defense Manpower Data Center, hackers went after the people who serve and support the military, not its weapons or its intelligence tools. An earlier intrusion into the center affected 2.76 million living people, a fraction of the more than 60 million people the agency held records on in fiscal 2024.

For the people in those files, the risk is personal. The exposed details include birthdates and military specialties, which together link who a person is to the work that person does for the military.

Intruders were inside the center's systems for months before anyone noticed. Unauthorized access began in October 2025, and no one found the weakness that let them in until July 16, 2026. No one has publicly named the attacker.

The people in those files may not learn for years whether anyone has used their details.

At Cloud One, the hackers did harm simply by getting in, and any theft that comes to light would only add to it.

The FBI suffered two breaches in one fall. The first came in September, when intruders took data on FBI employees and forced the agency to shut down part of its operations until the breach was resolved. The second reached the National Crime Information Center, a shared criminal-justice system that police well beyond the FBI rely on, so a breach there becomes a problem for every department that checks a name against it.

This breach puts everyday police records at risk, so what matters is whether departments can still trust what they look up. The September theft was the work of a cybercrime group called ShinyHunters, which shows criminal hackers, not only foreign governments, are getting inside federal law enforcement. No one has publicly named who broke into the criminal database.

When Trump talked about the database break-in, he spoke of a possible upside rather than the damage, suggesting the breach might turn up evidence of voter fraud. "I always like to put things on a positive spin," Trump said.

Police nationwide still rely on a system whose breach the government has acknowledged but not explained.

The 2026 breaches reached civilian departments and commercial ships as well as spy and military systems. Personnel data leaked from the Department of Homeland Security, intruders broke into the Treasury Department, and as many as 50 ships carrying oil and other explosive cargo are believed to have been hit by cyberattacks. No details have been made public on what the intruders reached at either department.

Iran is the primary suspect in the ship attacks, according to The Wall Street Journal, and U.S. officials also see Russia as a possible culprit. A Trump administration official disputed that, saying the U.S. has found no evidence of Iranian involvement and that four attacks amounted to little more than a minor nuisance. Coast Guard cyber teams have responded to at least four of the ships as they approached U.S. ports.

The attackers are exploiting a flaw in Fortinet $FTNT routers that are popular in the maritime industry. Some ships also received bomb threats, and the attacks come as Iran continues to mount physical attacks against ships in the Strait of Hormuz.

The ship attacks can't easily turn a tanker into a weapon, but a hacked vessel can still stall a cargo of fuel.

#5397. The Simple AI Framework I Use to Cut Administrative Waste

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

AI delivers the greatest business impact when it’s implemented strategically to eliminate repetitive administrative work, reduce burnout and free employees to focus on high-value, relationship-driven tasks.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

When I opened my first physical therapy practice, I believed growth depended on seeing more patients. That mindset worked for a while, until I realized my team and I were spending hours every day on paperwork, scheduling and insurance tasks instead of patient care. Administrative work had quietly become the biggest obstacle to growth.

Years later, after building therapy, staffing and hospice companies, I see artificial intelligence the same way I see any business tool: Its value comes from solving a real operational problem. AI should give your people more time to serve customers and build relationships. Everything else is secondary. That philosophy has shaped how we use technology across our businesses.

Spend a week identifying every repetitive task that eats up valuable time. Look for work that follows the same steps every day and requires little judgment. Those processes usually deliver the fastest return when automated.

In health care, charting, appointment scheduling and insurance verification quickly rose to the top of our list. Every industry has its own version of these tasks. Find them before you buy any technology.

Resist the urge to automate everything at once. Doing so can overwhelm you and your team, and it makes it hard to tell which changes worked and which flopped.

Start with the one to three administrative processes that consume the most hours each week. For us, documentation was the obvious first choice. AI-assisted transcription dramatically reduced the time clinicians spent writing notes, so they could focus on patients instead of keyboards.

We also introduced AI tools for scheduling and insurance verification. Those systems reduced delays and freed employees to handle conversations that required empathy and critical thinking.

Many leaders evaluate AI by asking whether the software costs less than another employee. I prefer a different question: How many productive hours did the technology return to the business?

If documentation falls from 30 minutes to five minutes per appointment, those recovered hours create measurable capacity. Teams can serve more customers, improve quality or simply leave work on time. Revenue often follows, but the first win is reclaimed time.

Tracking time savings also keeps expectations realistic. Every automation project should produce measurable improvements before you expand it to another department.

Every AI project deserves a simple scorecard. Track how many hours employees save each week, how quickly customers get a response, how many errors disappear from the process and how your team feels after the change. Those measurements show whether the technology is delivering real value or just adding another subscription to the budget.

Review these metrics every month. Small improvements often compound into significant operational gains over time. Consistent measurement also helps employees see the purpose behind each new tool, which builds confidence and speeds adoption across the organization.

Burnout rarely begins with meaningful work. It usually begins with repetitive work.

Few health care professionals entered the field because they loved paperwork, and entrepreneurs in every industry can relate. Endless administrative duties drain energy that could go to customers, employees or strategic planning.

When AI removes repetitive work, people get back to the work that inspired them in the first place, and burnout drops as a result. In our businesses, clinicians give more attention to patient conversations because documentation happens in the background. That shift improves both the employee experience and the customer experience.

Successful adoption comes from discipline, not speed. Begin with one department. Select one workflow. Define one success metric. Once that process delivers consistent results, move on to the next opportunity.

This phased approach builds confidence throughout the organization. Employees see practical improvements instead of another technology initiative that creates extra work. Leaders also gain reliable data before making larger investments.

Small wins create momentum that large transformations rarely achieve on day one.

One common misconception is that AI is meant to replace people. It isn’t.

Technology should strengthen human capability, not replace human judgment. Every automation decision we make comes back to the same question: Will this give our people more time for work that requires experience, compassion and creative thinking?

That principle has guided our investments, from AI documentation to administrative automation. Technology handles repetition. People handle relationships. Together, they build stronger businesses than either could alone.

Once we put these changes in place, the difference was almost immediate. Clinicians spent less time on documentation after appointments and more time engaging with patients during them. Front office teams fielded fewer routine calls because scheduling and administrative questions moved through AI-powered workflows, which reduced delays and made the experience smoother for everyone.

What surprised me most was the ripple effect. Employees felt less overwhelmed because they could focus on work that required their expertise. Leaders had better visibility into operations because we were measuring performance instead of reacting to problems. Those improvements gave us the confidence to expand AI into other areas of the business, one process at a time.

The experience reinforced something I’ve believed throughout my career: Sustainable growth comes from building systems that free talented people to do what they do best. AI became one more tool that helped us deliver better care, strengthen our operations and prepare our businesses for the next stage of growth.

When I opened my first physical therapy practice, I believed growth depended on seeing more patients. That mindset worked for a while, until I realized my team and I were spending hours every day on paperwork, scheduling and insurance tasks instead of patient care. Administrative work had quietly become the biggest obstacle to growth.

Years later, after building therapy, staffing and hospice companies, I see artificial intelligence the same way I see any business tool: Its value comes from solving a real operational problem. AI should give your people more time to serve customers and build relationships. Everything else is secondary. That philosophy has shaped how we use technology across our businesses.

Spend a week identifying every repetitive task that eats up valuable time. Look for work that follows the same steps every day and requires little judgment. Those processes usually deliver the fastest return when automated.

#5396. Trump has found something to blame for his midterm loss: ‘Fake’ growth numbers out of Howard Lutnick’s Commerce Department

The headaches just keep piling up for Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has been on his case about the Commerce Department’s handling of Nvidia, following the news of Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy. And now President Trump is blaming his team for publishing “fake” growth numbers before the midterms.“It was just revealed that the real numbers on the economy, published before the election, were fake, and a correction was issued yesterday by the people in the government agency that does these numbers,” the president posted on Truth Social.

“The American economy under the Trump administration is doing far better than the good numbers already released.”

The agency Trump appears to be referring to is the Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA), which sits within the Commerce Department.

The BEA operates with statistical and methodological independence, a safeguard designed to protect the accuracy and impartiality of its statistics.

On Wednesday, the BEA issued revisions to its growth figures for the third quarter of 2026, saying GDP was 4.3%—not the 3.9% it had originally forecast. The upward revision of 0.9% on the initial estimate was “primarily reflecting upward revisions to investment and consumer spending.”

Analysts are unlikely to be surprised. Revisions are a routine feature of U.S. economic statistics. Lower survey response rates have reduced the precision of some estimates. As UBS’s Pauk Donovan said in a note to clients this morning: “Changes in U.S. economic growth are exaggerated by the fiction of annualization (a technique employed by very few advanced economies).”

“Data revisions are more common as structural change and poor survey response rates reduce precision.”

But President Trump suggested there were more nefarious reasons for the near-percentage-point difference in initial estimates to the published figures: “Why wasn’t the correct number issued before the election? I am asking for an immediate investigation of this situation. This is not a small error, this is a massive, and purposeful, error.”

Lutnick issued a bullish economic update. Writing on X, the Commerce Secretary said: “We’re bringing American manufacturing back at a scale nobody thought possible. America’s successes will become even more powerful in the coming years as these projects move from groundbreaking to full production.”

Trump’s latest clash with federal data agencies could further undermine confidence in U.S. economic statistics. In 2025, the president fired the director of the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), Erika McEntarfer, claiming she had overseen the publishing of “phony” job numbers for political reasons. (The president provided no evidence for his claim.)

This, paired with Trump’s extraordinary attacks on the Federal Reserve under former chairman Jerome Powell, led many economists and investors to worry about the credibility of major U.S. institutions that either inform policy or make it.

At the time, Alberto Cavallo, Professor at Harvard Business School, told Goldman Sachs: “It’s difficult to avoid a comparison to the experience of my home country, Argentina, nearly two decades ago when the president, dismayed at rising inflation, removed statistical agency leadership.

“Some statistics stopped being reported, and official data no longer seemed to align with perceptions. That was a very chaotic period that destroyed trust in Argentina’s official statistics for over a decade.”

While Cavallo said the U.S. is ahead of some of Argentina’s data bodies in terms of skills and institutional checks and balances, he said the situation was still “very concerning.”

#5394. Buy now, pay later on Black Friday: 7 checks before you split a payment

Using buy now, pay later on Black Friday can make holiday deals easier to manage, but fees, due dates, returns and credit checks deserve a look first

A split payment changes when you pay for something, not what you owe for it. That distinction is easy to lose at checkout, where a pay-in-four button can make a large purchase look like a small one.

Black Friday is the day after U.S. Thanksgiving, which falls on the fourth Thursday of November. It opens a stretch of holiday shopping that runs straight into December bills. Retailers promote deals with short deadlines, and checkout pages often list installment plans alongside cards and digital wallets. Providers such as Klarna, Afterpay, Affirm and PayPal $PYPL appear at checkout on many retail sites, and some stores offer their own versions.

The basic model works like this. A pay-in-four plan divides a purchase into four equal payments. The first is due when you check out. The rest are collected on a set schedule, usually by automatic charge to a linked card. Longer plans stretch payments over months and can carry interest. Each provider writes its own terms, and those terms can change.

That variation is the reason to slow down before using buy now, pay later on Black Friday. Two plans that look identical on a product page can still differ. They may treat missed payments, returns and credit reporting in different ways. The answers sit in the provider's app and disclosures, not in the retailer's banner ad.

The checks below are meant to be done before you tap the button, not after the confirmation email arrives. They start with the total amount you will repay and how it compares with the sticker price. They move through late-fee rules, the timing of each installment against your paydays and the card that will be charged. They also cover how refunds work when an item goes back and how providers handle credit checks and reporting. The last covers how to keep track of several plans running at once.

Each check answers a specific question about a specific plan. The result is a checkout decision made with the full terms in view, rather than one made under the pressure of a sale clock.

Before agreeing to a buy now, pay later plan, compare the total you will repay with the sticker price of the item. If the two figures match, the plan changes only when you pay. If the total is higher, the difference is what the borrowing costs.

On a pay-in-four plan, the four installments together should equal the checkout price. If they add up to more, find out what the extra covers before confirming.

Longer plans can work differently. Monthly installment loans from providers such as Affirm can carry interest. Once interest applies, the payments added together can exceed the price on the tag. At the same rate, a loan that runs longer gives interest more time to build.

Rates differ by provider and by shopper. Two people buying the same television from the same retailer may be offered different terms. A rate seen on a friend's plan, or on an earlier purchase, says little about the offer on the screen today.

The check itself is simple arithmetic. Find the installment amount and the number of payments on the plan summary shown before you confirm. Multiply the installment amount by the number of payments. Then set that figure beside the full checkout price, including tax and shipping. If the multiplied figure is larger, the gap is the price of spreading the cost out.

Check the number of payments as closely as the amount. A plan with a smaller installment may simply run for more months. A lower monthly figure does not mean a lower total.

The comparison carries extra weight on discounted items. Black Friday sales are built around markdowns. Interest charged on a sale item eats into the discount. Depending on the rate and the length of the loan, it can shrink the saving or erase it. The fair comparison is the sale price paid outright, not the original price the retailer crossed out.

When the total repaid exceeds the sticker price, the shopper has a clear choice. One path is to accept that extra cost knowingly. The other is to pay a different way.

Know what a buy now, pay later provider does when an installment is missed before you split a Black Friday purchase. Klarna and Afterpay may charge late fees. Affirm has said it does not charge late fees.

A shopper who picks one of these providers at checkout is also picking the rules for the weeks after the sale. The missed-payment rules come from the provider's agreement with the shopper.

Fee policies can change. A provider can revise its terms. The version that applied to a purchase last year may not match the one in force this Black Friday. The reference that counts is the current agreement shown in the provider's app or disclosures at the time of purchase.

The word "may" in a fee summary matters too. Whether a fee applies to a specific order is set out in the current terms, not in a general description of the provider.

Reading that agreement means looking for a few specific answers. Does the provider charge anything for a missed installment? If it does, is the charge a flat amount or tied to the size of the order? Does the agreement set a limit on total fees for a single purchase?

Timing is the next thing to look for. Check whether the terms describe a window after a missed due date before any fee applies. Check whether the provider tries the charge again, and when. See whether a due date can be moved before it arrives.

A fee is not the only rule worth knowing. Look for what a missed payment means for using the same provider on later orders. The same app may appear at checkout again before the holiday shopping season ends.

Affirm's statement covers late fees only. It does not describe everything else in its agreement. The rest of its terms still need a full read.

A screenshot of the fee section taken at checkout creates a record of the rules shown when you agreed. That record helps if a question about a charge comes up weeks later. Keep it with the order confirmation.

Before splitting a Black Friday purchase, match each installment's due date to the day money actually lands in your account. The first payment comes out at checkout. The rest follow a schedule the provider sets, not one built around your pay cycle.

Many providers collect the remaining three installments about every two weeks. That pattern is common, but it is not universal. Schedules vary by provider. The exact dates appear at checkout and in the provider's app, and those are the dates that count.

On a two-week rhythm, the last payment lands roughly six weeks after the purchase. Black Friday falls in late November. A plan opened that day would run into early January.

That window matters because of what else sits inside it. December brings regular monthly bills, and often more holiday spending on top of them. A split payment taken on Black Friday adds three more draws across the same weeks. Putting them on a calendar before checkout makes the overlap visible.

The practical step is to write down your income dates for the next six weeks. Then place each installment date beside them. If an installment falls a day or two before a paycheck arrives, that payment has to come from money already in the account. If it falls just after payday, it competes with rent, utilities and other fixed costs due around the same time.

The first installment deserves separate attention. It is charged on Black Friday itself, whatever your pay schedule. A shopper paid at the end of the month may be near the bottom of the cycle when that charge hits.

Someone paid every two weeks may find the installments line up closely with paydays. Someone paid once a month may see most installments fall between paychecks. Neither pattern rules out a plan on its own. What matters is knowing which one applies before agreeing to the terms.

Do not assume a due date can be moved later. If a provider offers any way to change one, its terms will spell that out. Read them before relying on that option.

The card linked to a buy now, pay later plan determines what a short balance will cost. A debit card exposes the shopper to bank overdraft or declined-payment fees, while a credit card adds its own interest on any balance carried.

Installments on split-payment plans are usually charged automatically to the card the shopper links at checkout. Each later payment comes off that card on its due date, with no further action needed. The card chosen during a Black Friday checkout shapes what happens on every one of those dates.

A debit card draws directly on a bank account. The money leaves the account on the day the installment is collected, not the day the item was bought. If the balance is short on that day, the bank may cover the charge and apply an overdraft fee. It may instead refuse the charge and apply a declined-payment fee.

Those bank charges sit apart from the BNPL plan itself. A refused charge can also leave the installment unpaid. That brings the provider's own missed-payment rules into play. Reading both the bank's fee terms and the provider's terms covers each side of that risk.

The practical risk with debit funding is timing inside the account. Rent, utilities, subscriptions and other automatic debits may draw on the same balance in the same week. An installment that looked small at checkout can be the charge that pushes the account below zero.

A credit card moves the installments off the bank account, but it does not remove cost. Each installment joins the card's balance. If the shopper carries part of that balance from month to month, the card's interest applies to it.

That means a plan with no interest of its own can still end up costing interest. The card issuer charges that interest, not the BNPL provider. The card also has its own payment date, separate from the installment schedule.

Before confirming a split payment, a shopper can check which card the plan will charge and what that card's terms say about carried balances. For a debit card, the useful question is whether the linked account will hold enough on each collection date, not only on Black Friday itself.

A refund on a buy now, pay later purchase goes through the BNPL provider, not only the retailer. Installments may keep coming due until the return is processed. Read the store's return policy and the provider's refund process before you check out.

A split payment creates two separate relationships. The retailer decides whether an item can come back and how long you have to send it. The provider manages the loan, including how a refund is applied to your plan.

Start with the retailer. Find the return window for the specific item you are buying. Check whether the product page or receipt marks it as final sale or lists different conditions for discounted stock. Black Friday markdowns deserve this extra look before you commit.

Then turn to the provider. Its refund process explains what happens to an installment plan once the retailer accepts a return. Look for it in the provider's app or help pages before you agree to the plan, not after a package is already in transit.

The weak point is the gap between sending an item back and the refund posting. A return has to be shipped, received and processed by the retailer. Until that happens, scheduled payments may still be charged to your linked card. Budget for them as though you had kept the item.

Keep a simple paper trail for every split purchase you might return. That means the order confirmation, any return authorization, the shipping receipt and the tracking number. If a refund stalls, those records show when the item left your hands.

If a refund never arrives, or the retailer and provider give different answers, the next step is the provider's own dispute policy. Rules for disputing BNPL purchases in the U.S. have been subject to regulatory change. Do not assume a specific federal protection covers your purchase. Read the provider's current dispute terms, which set out how to raise a problem and what the provider will review.

Gifts bought on an installment plan need one more check. The plan belongs to the buyer, even if someone else sends the item back. Ask the recipient to tell you when they return it, then watch your plan for the adjustment.

Buy now, pay later providers differ on two credit questions: the type of credit check run at approval and whether the loan is reported to credit bureaus. Check both in the provider's disclosures before splitting a Black Friday purchase. One app's answer does not carry over to another.

The first question is about approval. Some buy now, pay later providers run a soft credit check when a shopper applies. Others run a hard credit check. The provider decides which one applies, and its own terms are the place to confirm it.

The second question is about what happens after approval. Some providers report their installment loans to credit bureaus, and some do not. That choice decides whether a plan appears on a shopper's credit file at all.

The two answers are independent. A provider can handle its approval check one way and its bureau reporting another. Each question needs its own look in the disclosures.

The practical step is to open the provider's app or website before checkout. Find the sections that cover credit checks and credit reporting. A sale-day checkout screen may show only the payment amounts. The credit details may sit somewhere else entirely.

When a retailer offers more than one split-payment option, the comparison can include these two points alongside the payment terms. Noting each provider's approach to checks and reporting keeps the options straight. That record also helps when the same shopper sees different providers at different stores over the holiday weekend.

There is no single answer to whether buy now, pay later hurts credit. The question has to be asked plan by plan. Reading that provider's disclosures is the reliable way to know what a specific plan involves.

If a provider's disclosures leave either question unanswered, that gap is something to weigh before agreeing to split the payment. The same check applies to any store-specific plan offered at checkout during Black Friday sales.

Before adding a new buy now, pay later plan during Black Friday sales, list every plan already running, with its next due date and remaining balance. That single tally shows what you already owe before another installment joins the queue.

Split payments are easy to stack. A shopper can hold plans with Klarna, Afterpay, Affirm and PayPal $PYPL at the same time, plus a store-specific option from a single retailer. Each plan runs on its own autopay date. None of them waits for the others.

That separation makes the total hard to see. Each provider's app shows the plans held with that provider. It does not show a pay-in-four plan opened elsewhere a week earlier. A shopper checking one app sees only part of what is owed.

The tally itself needs only three columns. The first names the provider and the item bought. The second records the next due date. The third records the balance still owed on that plan. A notes app, a spreadsheet or a sheet of paper all work.

Fill it in by opening each provider's app or account in turn. Copy the dates and balances directly from those screens rather than from memory. Include store-specific plans. They are easy to miss because they sit inside a retailer's own checkout or account.

Once the list is complete, add up the third column. That sum is the amount still due across every active plan. Then sort the rows by due date. The sorted list shows which days carry more than one payment and how closely the charges bunch together.

Only then look at the new purchase. Add it as a fresh row, with its own first payment and its own future dates. Compare the new total with the old one. If the new row lands on a date that already holds other payments, that clustering is visible before checkout rather than after.

Keep the list current through the rest of the holiday season. Plans opened over the Black Friday weekend can still be collecting payments well into December. Update a row each time a payment clears, and delete it when the balance reaches zero. A plan that is dropped from the list too early, or never added, leaves the total incomplete.

#5393. How To Build Influence Without Waiting for Authority

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Building influence requires more than a leadership title or strong job performance. By developing relationships, gathering evidence, earning trust and taking initiative, professionals can shape decisions, create meaningful change and establish themselves as leaders before receiving formal authority.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Early in my career, I believed excellent work would eventually create its own reward. I became the person people trusted to solve problems, take on difficult assignments and deliver when the stakes were high. Yet there is a trap hidden inside reliability: You can become indispensable to the work without becoming influential in the decisions that determine it.

I eventually learned to separate authority from influence. Authority comes with a title or responsibility for the final decision. Influence is your ability to move an idea, change an outcome or bring people with you regardless of what appears beneath your name in an email signature.

That distinction matters because waiting for authority can consume years. Influence can begin from almost any position, including one far from the executive table.

When I enter an organization as a consultant, I spend the early stretch watching. I want to understand who people consult before making a decision, whose objections carry weight and who has direct access to the person making the final call.

The organizational chart provides useful information, but it rarely shows the full picture. I think of the real structure as a web. To start mapping yours, study a few decisions and ask:

Write down what you observe. Look for patterns rather than focusing only on seniority. This helps you see where your relationships and contributions can have greater impact and where you may have been spending energy with little effect on the final outcome.

I learned this while working to improve outcomes for Black women inside an organization. During my first several months, I created programs, workshops and employee groups. Leadership was pleased, yet I could see that we were addressing individual women while leaving larger cultural problems untouched.

Instead of walking into an executive meeting and declaring that the approach needed to change, I gathered evidence. I examined exit interviews, studied promotion patterns, found allies prepared for deeper change and ran small pilots that demonstrated another approach.

By the time I pushed for a larger change, I had evidence, results and people behind me. Over roughly 18 months, the work became more strategic because I had built the influence required to change how the problem was understood.

Before making your next significant proposal, gather three things:

An idea becomes harder to dismiss when other people can see what you see. Building support early also gives people an opportunity to improve the idea before you bring it into a higher-stakes conversation.

Being excellent at your job creates credibility, but credibility alone can leave you with more assignments rather than greater impact. People know you will deliver, so they keep handing you things to deliver. Eventually, being the dependable person can become its own holding pattern.

Use the trust you have earned to shape the work itself. Propose an improvement, ask to participate earlier in a project or volunteer to lead an initiative that connects you with people outside your immediate team. Keep a record of problems solved, measurable outcomes and moments when colleagues sought your judgment.

Credibility sitting still makes you useful. Credibility applied to decisions expands your influence.

Many professionals concentrate their relationship-building efforts on senior executives. Yet influence rarely travels through a single relationship. Peers, colleagues in other departments, administrative professionals and people closer to customers can all help an idea move.

The Revolutionary Pathmakers I write about have historically created networks through community and cross-functional relationships when conventional pathways were unavailable. Those relationships provided information, support and opportunities that formal structures alone failed to provide.

This is not just history. My research found that Black women who lead from values rather than position build more sustainable authority than traditional power-based models, with higher retention and better long-term results. When the formal channels are closed, influence built through relationships and shared values is not the backup plan. It turns out to be the stronger one.

Identify two people outside your usual circle and learn what they are trying to accomplish. Ask what repeatedly creates difficulty for them and where your work intersects. Enter those conversations looking for ways to contribute rather than immediately asking for something.

Influence grows when people experience your contribution before you need their support.

I often coach people who describe having little power while simultaneously outlining solutions they can put into motion. The question I ask is simple: What can you responsibly begin from where you are?

You might test one part of an idea, improve a recurring process, connect people working separately or gather evidence around a problem nobody owns. Start small enough that the idea can prove itself, then document the result. Pay attention to what worked, who benefited and what would be required to expand it.

A successful experiment gives you something stronger than a proposal about what might work. It gives you evidence of what already did.

I spent years being excellent while being overlooked. What changed my trajectory was understanding that waiting for recognition was delaying the leadership I was already capable of practicing.

Influence grows when you understand how decisions move, build relationships before you need them, use your credibility intentionally and create opportunities to demonstrate what you can do. These actions can begin well before a promotion appears.

There is one more piece, and it may be the one that matters most. Moral clarity. The influence that lasts belongs to people who stand for something bigger than their own advancement. When you are clear about what you are for, and consistent about it, people follow you because of what you represent, not just what you can do for them. Authority can be granted. Moral authority has to be earned, and it is the kind no one can take back.

A title can expand your authority, but your ability to make an impact can begin long before anyone changes the words beneath your name. The question is whether you will wait for that change or start using the influence you already have.

Early in my career, I believed excellent work would eventually create its own reward. I became the person people trusted to solve problems, take on difficult assignments and deliver when the stakes were high. Yet there is a trap hidden inside reliability: You can become indispensable to the work without becoming influential in the decisions that determine it.

I eventually learned to separate authority from influence. Authority comes with a title or responsibility for the final decision. Influence is your ability to move an idea, change an outcome or bring people with you regardless of what appears beneath your name in an email signature.

That distinction matters because waiting for authority can consume years. Influence can begin from almost any position, including one far from the executive table.

#5392. In 2026, many employers are ditching merit-based pay bumps in favor of ‘peanut butter raises’

Professionals have long been taught a simple formula for career success: work hard, outperform your peers, and bigger paychecks will follow. But this year, employers are planning to reward their star staffers differently; instead of factoring in merit, more companies are considering general pay hikes spread out evenly, dubbed the “peanut butter raises” trend.

Around 44% of employers plan to roll out uniform, across-the-board wage bumps in 2026, according to a 2026 Payscale report. About 16% of organizations are newly implementing these “peanut butter” raises: 9% say they already employ the pay strategy, and another 18% of organizations are considering it this year. And top-performing companies are all-in on the approach. Around 56% of organizations that reported that they would exceed their revenue goals in 2025 are using or actively considering peanut butter pay increases.

Companies are still planning to boost employee pay by 3.5%, the same rate as last year. And while 48% of businesses will continue the tradition of awarding pay bumps based on worker performance—which the report described as a “best practice”—the new compensation fad may be trying to alleviate financial headwinds for low-paid workers.

“Tying merit pay increases to performance ratings has come under criticism in recent years for being too subjective and prone to bias,” the Payscale report noted. “At the same time, some organizations have made headlines by electing to standardize pay increases to alleviate administrative burden and reward workers equally, especially for low wage workers where inflation is a big concern.”

Job seekers and staffers alike are suffering through a difficult labor market: Hiring has slowed, layoffs are steadily streaming in, and wages don’t feel like they’re holding up. Looking at the year ahead, the picture doesn’t look too pretty.

Wall Street analysts and business executives have been floating the idea we’re in a “K-shaped economy”; higher-income Americans are witnessing their earnings and wealth rise, while lower-income people are struggling against smaller gains and the high cost of living. The concept has come to explain the confusing U.S. economy, where solid overall growth contrasts with sluggish hiring and rising unemployment.

While U.S. companies are holding their average salary increase budget steady at 3.5%, according to a 2025 report from Willis Towers Watson, there’s a large cohort that is planning to scale back. Nearly a third of businesses plan to lower their compensation-increase budgets compared to last year, citing a potential recession, dwindling financial performance, and desire for more control over costs.

Last year, one high-profile employer ditched its merit-based raises in favor of a general, flat pay bump. Starbucks announced it would be giving a standard 2% raise to all salaried North American employees in 2025, diverging from the norm that managers have a say in the raises of their direct reports. It was all a part of CEO Brian Niccol’s bid to reduce costs in a broader company turnaround effort.

But Starbucks is just one notable name in a growing list of employers hunkering down for economic hardship. Lexi Clarke, Payscale’s chief people officer, told Fortune last year that pay-increase budgets are being slimmed as tariffs and economic woes create uncertainty, forcing many employers to be on their guard.

“Economic concerns have now overtaken labor competition as the primary driver of compensation decisions,” Clarke said, as “66% of employers cite this as the reason for pulling back, up 17% from last year.”

As more companies trim back wage budgets and hand out peanut butter raises, there are many still reinvesting in their star talent. America’s largest private employer, $988 billion retail titan Walmart, unrolled a strategy in 2024 to pay its top store managers up to $620,000 per year.

U.S. CEO John Furner said it was a way to “make managers feel like owners,” acknowledging their success with a slice of the profit pie. Their average base pay was hiked from $130,000 to $160,000, raising their total compensation to between $420,000 and $620,000 annually.

And with more than 4,000 store managers across the U.S. (and around 1.5 million workers) when the policy went into effect, the payout wasn’t just generous—it was a calculated bet on culture.

A version of this story was published on Fortune.com on February 2, 2026.

Emma Burleigh is a reporter at Fortune, covering success, careers, entrepreneurship, and personal finance. Before joining the Success desk, she co-authored Fortune’s CHRO Daily newsletter, extensively covering the workplace and the future of jobs. Emma has also written for publications including the Observer and The China Project, publishing long-form stories on culture, entertainment, and geopolitics. She has a joint-master’s degree from New York University in Global Journalism and East Asian Studies.

#5391. Etzioni on AI: The outage conspiracy theories are wrong — our rush to patch and upgrade is the culprit

by Oren Etzioni on Nov 22, 2026 at 7:04 amNovember 22, 2026 at 7:06 am

In less than a week, Microsoft email went dark around the world, the FAA halted every departure in the country, Chase payments stalled, Apple’s services faltered and the NSA’s internal network went down. Sen. Josh Hawley said that if this was all a coincidence, “it’s like the greatest coincidence in the history of the world.” Yet intelligence and law enforcement officials told Congress they’ve found no evidence that anyone was attacking us.

Attackers typically announce when they’ve hit you. Terrorists claim credit. Criminals issue ransom notes and often brag as well: the hackers who crippled MGM’s casino systems in 2023 told TechCrunch within days. None of this month’s outages came with any of that.

Could a state actor be flexing its cyber capabilities to warn us? China’s Volt Typhoon hackers kept access to U.S. critical infrastructure for at least five years before anyone made it public, positioning themselves to disrupt it in a future crisis. However, hackers who are that patient don’t blow their cover by knocking out the world’s email. A warning shot also works only if the target knows who fired it, and we don’t have a credible suspect for a shooter here.

Each outage has a separate origin tracing back to the organization’s own systems: a new router a contractor was installing for the FAA, a bug Microsoft shipped in July, a software bug at Chase, an internal update at Apple, a patch at the NSA. To stage that, a single attacker would have to break into three companies and two federal agencies, disguise every intrusion as a routine mistake and leave nothing for investigators to find.

A far more credible root cause is the patch treadmill set at too high a speed: AI is finding security holes faster than anyone can safely fix them, and the rush to patch and upgrade is making everything more fragile. Think of an immune system in overdrive. It fights off infection, and sometimes it attacks healthy tissue. This month’s outages were a flare-up.

On Nov. 17, the startup Calif disclosed Java4Shell, a critical flaw in Java, the software platform used by government agencies and about 90% of Fortune 500 companies. Calif found it with OpenAI’s GPT-6 Cyber model. Oracle shipped a patch the same day, and a federal alert urged organizations to “immediately patch.”

Last month the same startup used OpenAI models to find a flaw in PHP, the programming language behind an estimated 70% of websites, and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton tied the NSA’s outage to the patching that followed. Microsoft alone fixed 1,413 vulnerabilities in October, more than its previous record for an entire year.

AI is forcing faster fixes. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella says his company’s outage came from a dormant bug, but he warned this week that AI-driven patching could bring more instability. AI has “allowed us to find these bugs and fix these bugs, but that means you’ve got to then patch them, and that creates instability,” he told CNBC.

A patch for a critical bank system might once have been tested for a week, he said at the New York Times DealBook Summit. Now it “needs to go instantly from being available to being patched in production because it’s being exploited in the wild.”

The FBI warned on Nov. 13 that criminals and state-backed hackers are already using ARTEX, an open-source AI tool built for testing a company’s own defenses, with some intrusions going from first targeting to administrator-level access in under three hours. So the patching can’t slow down. Nobody would give up their immune system to avoid a flare-up.

It will get worse before it gets better. Calif’s CEO, Thai Duong, expects Java4Shell to threaten systems that don’t update for the next five to 10 years.

Meanwhile, the AI that finds flaws like this one is spreading. Open-weight models, which anyone can download and run without safeguards, trail the most advanced models on cyber tasks by only four to seven months, according to the UK AI Security Institute. Every month will bring more bugs, more emergency patches and more flare-ups.

There’s a finite amount of code in Windows, iOS and Chrome, and every bug AI finds and fixes there is one an attacker can’t use. Partners in Anthropic’s Project Glasswing, a program to secure critical software before AI can be turned against it, found more than 10,000 high- or critical-severity bugs in its first month.

Former Microsoft security staffer Angela Gunn sees a hopeful sign: more and more unrelated researchers are turning up the same bugs, which suggests the supply is finite. Fixing still lags finding, but the giants have the money and people to catch up. Within a year or two, I expect Windows, iOS and Chrome to be more secure than they’ve ever been.

#5389. Dow rallies nearly 600 points to close out its best week since 2022

The S&P 500 gained more than 5% and the Nasdaq more than 6% for the week, which ended with an early close

The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 591.99 points, or 1.2%, to close at 50,774.94 on Friday. That was the index's steepest one-week climb since October 2022, according to CNBC.

The S&P 500 climbed 1.6%, settling at 7,297.49, and a 2.3% rise lifted the Nasdaq $NDAQ Composite to 24,129.50. U.S. markets were closed Thursday for Thanksgiving and shut at 1 p.m. ET on Friday.

Technology stocks led the rebound. Meta $META Platforms stock rose more than 3%, Amazon $AMZN stock gained about 4% and Broadcom $AVGO stock climbed close to 4%.

For the week, the Dow and the S&P 500 each gained more than 5%, and the Nasdaq gained more than 6%. The S&P 500 turned in its strongest week since April 2025, and the Nasdaq posted its largest weekly gain since April, according to CNBC.

The week began with Nvidia $NVDA reinstating Jensen Huang as CEO. Nvidia stock jumped 31% on Monday, and the Dow gained over 1,400 points, or 3%. The S&P 500 and Nasdaq each logged their strongest one-day performance since April 2025 on Monday, according to CNBC.

Nvidia and other artificial-intelligence names have since surrendered a portion of that advance, dragging on the S&P 500 and Nasdaq, according to CNBC.

Huang left the company earlier this month. Before his departure, sentiment on AI stocks had already soured, according to CNBC, because investors were uneasy about how the buildout is funded with debt, indications that companies were trimming capital spending, and an expected slowing of data center construction following Democratic victories in the midterm elections.

Some market participants attribute the recent weakness more to the prospect of Federal Reserve interest rate increases, according to CNBC. Traders' expectations of several rate increases in the months ahead were strengthened by this week's newest personal consumption expenditures price index data.

#5388. I have a front-row seat to Norway’s cutting-edge AI newsroom experiment. Even with AI on more than 200 stories a day, a human still checks every one

Christoph Trattner is a professor of information science at the University of Bergen and the founding director of SFI MediaFutures, a research center for responsible media technology. Schibsted Media and Bergens Tidende are partners in the center and help fund it, and he is preparing a funding application with Fjell-Ljom.

Every day, Norway’s largest newspaper, VG, asks an AI model to suggest a headline, search terms and other details for each of its roughly 200 new articles. Before a journalist sees anything, a second model checks the first. In October, across all the newsrooms that use the system, it rejected about one in six of the first model’s attempts. Then the journalist checks the suggestion, and so does an editor, depending on how the newsroom is set up. The cheapest checker goes first, and the people who answer for the story still go last.

“Keep a human in the loop” has become the standard answer to AI’s mistakes. I wanted to know what that human costs, so I asked three Norwegian news organizations what it takes, and whether that has gone up or down as the tools improved. What I learned is that the cost of a check depends heavily on who does it, and on how close that person is to the original work.

I direct a research center on media technology in Norway, where newsrooms began publishing AI-written summaries in 2023. The answers come from the AI Foundations unit at Schibsted Media, the group that owns VG and the regional daily Bergens Tidende; from an editor at Bergens Tidende; and from an editor at Fjell-Ljom, a small local paper in the mountain town of Røros. I am not a neutral observer here: Schibsted Media and Bergens Tidende are partners in my center and help fund it, and I am preparing a grant application with Fjell-Ljom.

Nobody had a measured figure, and the numbers that exist elsewhere come from surveys, not stopwatches. But in one newsroom I could set the check against the work it replaces.

At Bergens Tidende, known as BT, reporters publish 15 to 20 stories of their own a day. AI is not, for now, permitted to write them, but it does write a short version of the finished story, which the reporter is responsible for checking before an editor checks it too. Jan Stian Vold, BT’s development editor, estimates that a reporter who knows the story needs anything from a few seconds to a couple of minutes, and that the editor’s look adds a minute or two. Writing the short version by hand, he told me, takes a reporter three to five minutes. These are his estimates, not measurements. Still, for the person who wrote the story, checking the machine’s version takes less time than writing one.

Vold’s guess is that about one short version in ten needs a fix, and he says the summaries have kept improving with the models. The usual problem is clumsy grammar, or a summary that misses what the reporter considers the most important point. “Almost never hallucinations,” he wrote to me. As far as BT knows, it has never published a critical mistake this way.

Office workers describe something different. In a Workday survey of 3,200 employees who use AI at large companies, nearly 40% of the time AI saved was lost to rework. In a survey of 1,150 U.S. employees by researchers at BetterUp and Stanford, each piece of workslop, AI-generated work that looks finished and is not, took nearly two hours to deal with. These are self-reports about longer documents, not a like-for-like comparison with a newsroom summary. But one difference stands out. In the office, the check often falls to someone who did not do the work and first has to find out what a right answer would look like. At BT, it falls to the one person who already knows.

A Georgia Tech researcher argued this month that catching AI’s mistakes is a mental burden that eats the gains. In the one newsroom where I could estimate it, the check took less time than the writing it replaced, and the reason is who does the checking.

Johanna Johansson, who works in AI Foundations at Schibsted Media, told me that “hallucinations are surprisingly common.” Vold had written “almost never.” Both can be right. She was speaking of AI-generated content in general, he of one narrow task, the summary of a text the reporter has just finished. Two things may be at work here, and I cannot separate them: a narrow task may produce fewer errors, and a checker who knows the material may spot the ones that remain faster.

On one point they agree. “Generally we always have a human in the loop,” Johansson said. That was always a firm principle, she said, and the huge improvements in the models have not made it any less important.

A judgment call, I would add, is the kind of error that only someone who knows the story is likely to notice.

So has the checking gone up or down? For BT’s newsroom as a whole, Vold could not say. His own work is administration and presentations, not journalism, and there his checking has gone down as he has learned to use AI as an assistant and not as a source of facts. At Fjell-Ljom it has stayed constant, because it was never a separate step. What nobody described is letting go of the check on what gets published.

I think they are right to hold that line, and the reason goes beyond the errors that remain. The check at BT is cheap because of everything the reporter did before the summary appeared. Hand the same summary to someone who had not reported the story, and the check would either take far longer or turn into a formality. A freelance journalist interviewed for a 2025 master’s thesis at Aalto University made a similar point: typing out an interview word for word “really gets you inside it in a way that reading over a transcription and just checking for errors doesn’t.”

For companies outside the news business, I take three things from this. Count the check: how many items, how many people look at each one, and how many minutes each look takes. Then set that against what the task took before. Do not treat a falling error rate as permission to stop checking. Nobody I asked has. Above all, give the check to the person who knows the work, instead of adding a reviewer downstream who has to start from nothing. In these newsrooms, that is what keeps the check manageable.

As AI takes over more of what comes before the check, I would worry less about the minutes than about whether anyone is left who can tell in seconds that something is wrong.

AI disclosure: The author drafted this piece with Claude (Anthropic), working from his interview notes and the newsrooms’ emails, and used it to search for and check the published studies cited. The reporting and the argument are his own, and he takes responsibility for the text.

#5387. Beyond Nvidia: Convoy co-founder and former Microsoft leader raise $277M to rethink AI infrastructure

by Todd Bishop on Nov 23, 2026 at 4:30 amNovember 23, 2026 at 1:27 pm

Former Microsoft executives Dan Lewis and Kutta Srinivasan have raised $277 million on a bet that the next wave of AI will run on a very different kind of data center.

The outsized seed funding for their new startup, Marlowe, reflects the scale of the challenge they’re taking on. As AI shifts from training models to running them in everyday products, Marlowe designs and operates computing systems for that work. It’s starting with chips from AMD and Etched, expanding beyond the Nvidia GPUs that have fueled the AI boom.

They say tuning the chips, networking and software for specific AI workloads and applications will maximize performance and efficiency, lowering costs as a result.

The new funding values Marlowe at $1.15 billion, according to the company, making it a unicorn out of the gate. Accel led the latest round, joined by a long list of big names in tech and finance, from KKR co-founder Henry Kravis to Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi.

Lewis, Marlowe’s CEO, previously co-founded the trucking startup Convoy and later was an enterprise AI leader at Microsoft, where Srinivasan, now Marlowe’s CTO, was a corporate vice president and the company-wide technical lead for AI infrastructure.

“The demand for intelligence and AI is very high,” Lewis said in an interview, when asked how a former freight marketplace CEO ended up in AI computing. “It’s something that should be accessible and affordable for everyone.”

Marlowe, founded in May, is based in both Bellevue, Wash., and Redwood City, Calif., and is approaching 30 employees. Lewis said the two home bases reflect where its customers, partners and talent are concentrated, pointing to Bellevue as an emerging AI hub.

Lewis, a former Amazon general manager, joined Flexport as a technical advisor when the freight company acquired Convoy’s technology after the startup’s abrupt shutdown in 2023. In February 2025, he returned to Microsoft, where he had also worked previously, as a chief product officer focused on enterprise AI, later becoming a corporate vice president.

GeekWire first reported in June that he had left Microsoft to launch a new startup, but he wasn’t ready to share details at the time.

From Microsoft to Marlowe: The founders said the idea for Marlowe grew out of what they saw at Microsoft: demand was surging for inference, running AI models in products and services, but data centers were still being built mainly for training those models in the first place.

“We were always oversold, effectively sold out,” Lewis said.

Since then, demand for inference has grown faster than supply, pushing up costs at the same time that power shortages, permitting and financing are making new data centers harder to build. The company cites a 40% increase in data center construction costs since 2020, which makes every watt more valuable.

The company isn’t using Nvidia chips for now, but it hasn’t ruled them out.

Its first site, built around Etched’s chips, is scheduled to go live in December, the founders said. A second, larger site using AMD’s new Helios systems is on track for the second quarter of 2027.

Both sites are under contract, and a third is under a letter of intent. The company says it has signed three customer agreements but isn’t yet naming the customers or the locations.

Srinivasan said that at the big tech companies where he has worked, chips from vendors other than Nvidia made up a small slice of the fleet. When a new AI model came out, the top engineers focused on getting it running on the Nvidia chips, and the rest got left behind.

“There were literally times when a significant portion of our non-Nvidia fleet was either idle or grossly underused or didn’t support the latest models and workloads,” he said.

That’s the gap Marlowe is trying to close. Its engineers work directly on customers’ workloads to get other chips performing at their full potential, giving those companies a way to reduce their dependence on a single supplier.

Marlowe says gains of 10% to 20% at each layer of the system, from chips and networking to power management and software, add up to two to three times more output per watt and per dollar than conventional GPU clouds, measured in tokens, the chunks of text that AI models process and generate.

Competition and funding: Marlowe isn’t alone in the bet. Gimlet Labs, which raised $300 million at a $3 billion valuation in September, and General Compute, which raised $100 million in October, are also building inference clouds that run on a mix of chips.

CoreWeave, the largest of the so-called neoclouds, rents out computing power built almost entirely on Nvidia chips. Nvidia held about 47 million CoreWeave shares as of Sept. 30, and CoreWeave has taken on about $47 billion in debt to build out its data centers.

Marlowe’s launch also comes during a turbulent stretch for Nvidia. The company’s board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO on Monday, less than two weeks after his resignation.

Much of Marlowe’s funding will go toward chips, networking equipment and the support needed to run the sites, along with hiring, the founders said. By the standards of AI infrastructure, $277 million doesn’t go far.

Rather than chasing giant facilities, Marlowe plans to prove its approach at sites of tens of megawatts and then finance more capacity site by site, Lewis said. He noted that some startups have raised four to five times as much and will deploy a little less computing power on a similar timeline.

The $277 million includes a smaller initial round led by Eclipse, Lewis said. Eclipse founder and CEO Lior Susan is Marlowe’s executive chairman, and Ido Susan, founder and CEO of the data center networking company DriveNets, is on the board. Other backers include Bessemer, Altimeter, Atreides, Journey and Valor.

Angel investors also include Box CEO Aaron Levie and former LinkedIn CEO Ryan Roslansky. Mark Okerstrom, the former Expedia CFO and CEO who later served as Convoy’s president, is also an investor.

Past lives: Srinivasan’s career runs from video games to AI infrastructure. In an earlier stint at Microsoft, he worked on DirectX and games including Halo 3, then spent eight years at Valve, where he led the team that built the first Steam mobile app.

He later served as the lead architect for machine learning training infrastructure at Facebook, and as a technical fellow at LinkedIn before moving to Microsoft’s CoreAI group in 2025.

Marlowe is a very different business from Convoy, the digital freight marketplace Lewis co-founded to match truckers with shippers. Convoy reached a $3.8 billion valuation before shutting down in 2023, amid a freight recession and a pullback in venture funding.

Asked how Marlowe would avoid getting similarly squeezed by forces outside its control in a capital-intensive business, Lewis said the industry is at “the very beginning” of a long-term shift in how people use AI and data.

He also pointed to a mix of long- and short-term contracts and multiple customers, rather than one big customer that could pull out.

Ultimately, Lewis said he believes Marlowe’s edge will come down to having the engineering skills to get the most out of new chips. “You can’t just take a new chip that comes out and plug it in and expect it to produce tokens,” he said. “You have to go do the work.”

Updated at 6:20 a.m. PT with Nvidia’s reinstatement of Jensen Huang as CEO.

#5386. Hackers breach Air Force's Cloud One: What's at risk and what's still unknown

Anonymous sources say hackers breached Cloud One, the Air Force's flagship cloud. Six slides separate what is confirmed from what is still unknown.

For years, the U.S. military has moved software off scattered computer systems and onto shared cloud platforms that are easier to manage but give attackers one larger target. The Air Force's flagship version is Cloud One, and hackers have now reportedly gotten inside it, Reuters reports. Cloud One's leaders had claimed a 100% success rate at repelling penetration attempts in a 2023 FedScoop commentary, according to the same report.

The breach's investigators have asked Cyber Command to help measure the harm. No one has established who the hackers are, how far they went or whether they took any data.

Cloud One brings Microsoft $MSFT, Amazon $AMZN, Oracle $ORCL and Alphabet $GOOGL under a single Air Force platform, so users reach all four companies' computing through one system. The Air Force started it in 2017, and Leidos has held the main contract to run it since 2025, replacing SAIC. Nothing on the record connects that change of contractor to the intrusion.

One platform means one place to manage, and one place to break into.

The Air Force's munitions-tracking software, the Theater Integrated Combat Munitions System, runs on Cloud One and keeps count of weapons at more than 200 sites around the world. So does Cloud-Based Command and Control, which pulls radar and other feeds into a single air-defense picture of North America. Nothing reported so far places the intruders inside either system.

These systems mark the outer limit of what the breach could cost.

One of five unnamed sources said the intruders used a software flaw to reach Cloud One's control plane, the layer that runs the whole platform. Access at that level could let an intruder check which aircraft are ready to fly and follow where spare parts are being shipped. No specific flaw has been identified, so no one outside the investigation can confirm it has been fixed.

The control-plane claim is the gravest risk in the breach, and it rests on a single source.

The Air Force has paused plans to move back-office software onto Cloud One and frozen updates to the applications already there, so teams can't patch them even as major new software flaws surface across the industry. Some users have also lost administrator access. The Air Force said it "does not comment on the security posture, vulnerabilities or operational status of specific networks and systems."

The clearest damage so far is a platform the Air Force can't fully use.
